speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I rise to a question of privilege.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext:
We are not on the
orders of the day yet.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext:
I draw your attention, sir,
to citation 170:
It is the practice in the House of Commons to bring up a question of privilege after prayers, and before the house has taken up the orders of the day.
Therefore I am in order.
My question of privilege is based on an article appearing in the Halifax Chronicle of February 4, which contains reference to proceedings which took place in this house on Friday last on the debate concerning the reestablishing of the lobster fishermen in their industry. It is headed, "Premier answers Ottawa comment," and goes on to say:
For more than eight years "the overwhelming majority of those unemployed in Canada or those otherwise in unfortunate economic circumstances have declared they prefer work to doles," Premier Angus L. Macdonald of Nova Scotia said to-night.
He was commenting on a discussion in the federal house to-day on the Nova Scotia government's plan to provide a "road works project" for fishermen who lost pots and equipment in November and December gales.
Repeatedly labour unions or associations, unemployed groups, social workers and others have urged that work be provided wherever possible. In the case of the storms in November and December in Nova Scotia the Nova Scotia government has endeavoured to pursue this policy. It endeavoured to provide work instead of doles or hand-outs.

If this can be called throwing a monkey wrench into the machinery, the government here is prepared-

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext:
Order. Would the hon.
member state his question of privilege?

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext:
The question of privilege is
that the premier of Nova Scotia has absolutely misrepresented me in saying that I threw a monkey wrench into the machinery, I being in favour of the dole. Nothing of the sort. I made my position on that point very clear in the debate in this house. In a letter which I addressed to His Honour the Speaker on the moving of the adjournment of the house on February 3, 1939, I said:
The provision of the Unemployment and Agricultural Assistance Act, 1938, is abortive in its provisions to meet the absolute need of reestablishing the said fishermen in their industry, and to provide them with the means of earning their livelihood, and to enable them to provide the bare necessities of life for their families.
During the debate I said:
But a monkey wrench was thrown into the machinery by the premier of Nova Scotia . . .
Then the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) in the debate on my motion on February 3, said:
Since this parliament, for the last three years at least, has deemed it advisable by supplementary appropriations to grant sums of money to help reestablish needy fishermen in their occupations . . .
And he adds that these moneys have always been distributed in the provinces where there was the need.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the premier of Nova Scotia goes on further to say, and it is a direct charge against myself, that I was not in Halifax when the storm took place, and that I had not any information in reference to it; in fact his inference is that I do not know the needs of my constituency.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext: The storm took place in the house.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext:
Well, perhaps a storm did take place when I spoke, but a tremendous gale takes place when the hon. member who has just interrupted me rises-or perhaps something more in the nature of a cyclone.
I may say for the information of the house that I was here in Ottawa for nearly four weeks in November attending to departmental matters with the various departments and again on December 8 after the December gale, conferring with the Minister of Fisheries.

Bren Gun-Ruling

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member has stated very well his point of privilege.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext: Perhaps that is your honour's opinion, but it is not mine.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext: I think the house is satisfied, so I would ask the hon. member to resume his seat.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman has made his point of privilege clear to the house and to the country, and in justice to himself I would ask him to resume his seat.

maintopic: NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHING INDUSTRY- ARTICLE IN HALIFAX CHRONICLE OF FEBRUARY 4

If that message will rebound
from here to Nova Scotia I shall be satisfied.

BREN MACHINE GUN CONTRACT

speakeroldname: Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: BREN MACHINE GUN CONTRACT
speechtext: I table herewith the return asked for last evening by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart), containing the agreement, a copy of which he requested, and also a letter referring thereto.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, February 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mac-Neil:
That the agreement between the government and the John Inglis Company, of Toronto, for the manufacture of Bren machine guns, the report of the royal commission dealing with said agreement, and all related documents, evidence, vouchers and exhibits, be referred to the standing committee on public accounts; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Manion.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before the debate proceeds I think this would be the appropriate time for me to render my decision on the point of order raised yesterday in regard to the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion).
The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) has moved to refer to the public accounts committee the Bren gun agreement, the report of the royal commission dealing with said agreement, and all related documents, evidence, vouchers and exhibits.
The hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has moved as an amendment that the said agreement be cancelled.
The motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North proposes to refer the agreement to the public accounts committee. The amendment proposes to cancel it, thus defeating the purpose of the main motion.
Bren Gun-Ruling

Can the motion be amended in the manner proposed? I do not think so. In the parliamentary debates of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, 4th series, volume 146, at page 990, I find that a motion was made for the appointment of a select committee-
-to consider the agreement of the 2nd day of February, 1905, between the Postmaster General and the National Telephone Company, and to report whether it is desirable in the public interest that the agreement should become binding. (Lord Stanley.)
Mr. Kearley (Devonport) proposed as an amendment that -
[DOT]-having regard to the public statement of the Postmaster General, under no circumstances can any alterations be made in the agreement with the telephone company to which he has given his assent, this house fails to see the necessity for the appointment of a committee to consider it.
The deputy speaker ruled:
I may point out to the hon. gentleman that this amendment will not be in order. It is a direct negative, but he will be at liberty to make his speech.
In the light of this decision I believe that the amendment proposed by the hon. the leader of the opposition for the cancellation of the agreement destroys the object of the main motion, when an alternative proposition is not permissible, and is in the nature of an expanded negative. I must therefore rule it out of order.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Without reflecting in any way upon yourself, Mr. Speaker, under the circumstances I feel it my duty to appeal from your ruling.	*
Mr. Speaker put the question as follows:
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) having proposed an amendment to the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) and Mr. Speaker having decided that the said amendment was out of order, Mr. Manion appeals to the house from the said decision of the speaker.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was paired with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Baker). Had I voted I would have voted to sustain Mr. Speaker's decision.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment last evening I had said a few words about the actions of the interdepartmental committee in connection with this contract. I pointed out during the course of my remarks that the promoters of this company had paid $100,000 for 191,662 shares of vendors' stock. This stock had a value of $6 per share, or $1,149,972, showing a profit of at least $1,049,972. The value of these shares had been established by the sale of treasury stock to the public at from $6 to $7.50 a share. Either the promoters made a profit of at least $1,049,972 or the public which purchased these treasury shares was gypped.
I should like to know whether these facts were brought to the attention of the interdepartmental committee when they were asked to give their opinion as to the advisability of giving this contract to Major Hahn and his associates. Did they know what profit was to be made by this promotion? Were they told that the promoters were to use not more than $500,000 in cash-the amount that was necessary to purchase the Inglis plant and provide working capital-to put this plant in production? I understand that under the contract the contractors are to receive ten per *cent on all machinery which goes into the
plant. The real money to be used in the production of these guns is only $500,000. I submit that if the interdepartmental committee had known that, there would have been no doubt as to their decision as to whether this contract should be awarded to Major Hahn and his associates, whether tenders should be called for, or whether the guns should be manufactured in our own arsenal. I am sure they would have decided that it was unnecessary for the government to allow a contractor a profit of $1,049,972 simply by his being awarded a contract. If they had known the small amount of money required to do this work they would have said: The government will manufacture these guns because the government can borrow money at three per cent for this purpose.
Going a little further, the interdepartmental committee were told that the British government had picked a contractor and would deal with no other firm. Now who was it that picked this contractor? The Prime Minister of this country picked him. He appointed him, by cable, to be Canada's representative. I say that the firm of John Inglis Company was forced on the British government, as shown by all the records, all the correspondence, and all the telephone conversations, code messages, and so forth, contained in the commissioner's report, and because of that the interdepartmental committee's hands were tied; for they were told that the British government would deal with no other firm.
Now let us look at the background of Major Hahn. He has an excellent war record. I do not know him personally but I hear that he is a very fine man. In the evidence it is pointed out that in 1934 the claims of the creditors of his company amounted to around $140,000. Over-expansion and the depression no doubt were the causes of the company's difficulties at that time, and that is not to his discredit. He compromised with his unsecured creditors for twenty cents on the dollar, and then sold out the assets of his company to the Rogers company, guaranteeing the payment of twenty cents on the dollar of his company's $140,000 of liabilities. The shareholders of his own company received one share in the Rogers company for ten shares of Major Hahn's company.
Again I say I have nothing against Major Hahn. I am just stating what is in the evidence. But this is the successful business man who was given carte blanche to the British war office with respect to Bren guns, and given access to all the secrets that he must have in order to make a contract with Great Britain for these guns. Again I ask,

Bren Gun-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
why was he picked by the British government? It is said that there may have been some delay in connection with the manufacture of these guns. It is said by some people that there may have been some detrimental factors with respect to receiving orders from the British government. I say now, Mr. Speaker, that the facts with respect to this contract, and the stock-jobbing that went on in connection with it, were bound to come to light sooner or later, and how much more it would have been to Canada's discredit to have them come to light later instead of coming to light and being settled now! Let us cancel this contract and get our credit with Great Britain straightened out. Let us start the manufacture of these guns ourselves, in our own arsenals, and make them without a profit. If we do that, I am perfectly certain that we shall get orders from Great Britain to make Bren guns for her, if we can do the job properly, and we ought to be able to do it with the brains and ability we have here.
As I said before, this is strictly a stockjobbing promotion from start to finish, based on profits accruing from the manufacture of implements of war, and every hon. member of this house knows it. All that the promoters had to find was an old building and a payroll to a matter of $500,000. The government paid for the machinery, and the government could just as easily have found that $500,000 and used it for putting a government arsenal into production. That would have saved ten per cent commission, as well, on the purchase of all the machinery which was going into this plant.
What about the actual cost of production of these guns? We hear rumours from time to time about the cost of production, running all the way from $250 up to $1,500 and $1,600. I do not know how much they cost, but I do know that there are plenty of industrial experts in this country who could give us an accurate estimate of the cost of producing them. There would be no difficulty in that, and if it was pointed out to our manufacturers that these guns are vital to Canada, I do not think there is a single industrial concern in this country which would not be only too glad to offer its services with respect to cost. Furthermore I am perfectly sure there is not a single one of these firms that would not be glad to give every bit of advice it possibly could with respect to putting a factory of this kind into operation.
There is a "but" to that, a great big "but," and that is patronage. You will not get cooperation from any industry in this country so long as there is patronage in the Department of National Defence, patronage in con-

nection with the awarding of contracts for the instruments of war-a profit of $1,049,972. The safety of our democracy is at stake. We must have no such patronage in the Department of National Defence. Democracy is founded on votes. Votes are being coerced through patronage. The Canadian taxpayer is paying for the patronage, and by that our democracy is endangered. Let us cancel the contract.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, during the course of
the summer I received a gift from Maclean's magazine. It was a reprint of the article published by Mr. George Drew, of notorious fame. He did not proceed in the article by means of accusations. He proceeded in the article, just the same as he did before Judge Davis, by insinuations. His article of nearly four pages contains two paragraphs referring to one of our esteemed colleagues in the House of Commons. I shall read them because at the time I was under the impression that the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) had been guilty of some kind of misdemeanour or offence; against the House of Commons Act. There is nothing worse, Mr. Speaker, than to proceed by insinuation, because you do not know what the accuser means by his insinuations. If there is a direct accusation, you can answer it; but there is nothing worse than putting doubts into the minds of the people.
Here are paragraphs 12 and 13 of the conclusion of the article:
12.	How does the government explain the fact that four of the seven directors of this enterprise are employees in the office of Plaxton and Company ?
13.	What is the position of Mr. Hugh Plaxton. M.P., in the office of Plaxton and Company, and what has it been at all times since Plaxton and Company began acting for the armament company which now has the contract?
This is the insinuation that was made by that notorious George Drew who, by the way, is a very good looking fellow-but there is no beauty contest to-day. In connection with these paragraphs 12 and 13 of the conclusion of this article we must read four paragraphs of the report made by Commissioner Davis, one of the learned judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. I was really surprised when I read that part of the report of Commissioner Davis, because it destroys entirely the whole insinuation of which George Drew himself was guilty. He was the guilty party in the matter.
Now let us give the Honourable Mr. Justice Davis an opportunity to remove all doubt concerning the integrity not only of the hon.

Bren Gun-Mr. Pouliol
member for Trinity but of all members of the government and of all members of this house. At this point I must say, before reading what Mr.. Justice Davis has to say, that the members of the House of Commons must be proud of the fact that they have been exonerated by a judge who is supposed to have no political affiliations and who was appointed by the Tories themselves. This is what Mr. Justice Davis has to say:
There is no evidence that any member of the senate or of the House of Commons of Canada was admitted to any share or part of the contract, or to any benefits to arise therefrom, or had been promised or given any suggestion that he was to have any share or part of the contract or was to be admitted to any share or part of the contract, or to any benefit to arise from the contract.
The evidence relating to the activities of Mr. Hugh Plaxton prior to the making of the contract has already been set out or referred to in this report, and with that exception (and excepting of course the minister presiding over the Department of National Defence) there is no evidence-
Mark you, there is no evidence.
-that any member of the senate or of the House of Commons of Canada had any connection with or took any part in the discussions or negotiations leading up to the contract.
There is no evidence that any senator or member had any connection with or took any part in the affairs of the company or in the sale of shares or securities of the company.
I think it right to say that there is no evidence (nor is there in the evidence any ground for suspicion) that the minister or the deputy minister or any officer or official of the Department of National Defence was guilty of any act of corruption or anything in the nature of corruption.
I have just this to add to the mention of the name of the deputy minister of national defence. All those who were with him at the front-and my brother was three years with him; he was wounded at Yimy when under his command-speak very highly of the integrity, the ability and the efficiency of the deputy minister of national defence, General LaFleche; and the way in which Colonel Drew proceeded against him was absolutely shameful. There are, of course, other officials of the Department of National Defence to whom I cannot pay the same compliment. General LaFleche is straightforward and honest, and he has that great quality which we do not always find among the chief officials of all departments of the government. He is loyal to his minister and he has been all the time. He has a splendid military record, but I will not insist on that.
Now here is the report. It speaks for itself; and of course if I read what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) said yesterday,
Judge Davis is an honourable man. I do not know him personally, but I presume he is.
I have the word of my hon. friend for it that he is. At page 641 of Hansard of yesterday the leader of the opposition made this statement :
With one of his remarks, to the effect that in appointing Mr. Justice Davis he was sure he had selected as commissioner one who would be satisfactory to the country, I am in complete accord.
In the words I have just quoted the leader of the opposition was referring to the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The hon. gentleman then goes on at page 703:
Now to deal with the report itself. When it first came out, indeed before it was made public, information was given through the press, I do not know by whom, that the report was a complete exoneration of the government as far as the Bren gun contract was concerned. To my mind that was merely propaganda. Far from this report being a complete exoneration of the government and those associated with the giving of this contract, it seems to me it is a complete condemnation of the government, as I shall prove before I finish. It is true that there was no evidence of corruption, but no one had charged corruption.
Observe, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman says that no one had charged corruption. It is true there was no evidence of corruption.
It is true that there was no evidence of corruption, but no one had charged corruption. I do not charge anything in the way of corruption now.
We do not find the assertion only in the words of Mr. Justice Davis; we find it on the lips of the leader of the opposition, and what the hon. gentleman says confirms all that I have stated, that Colonel Drew had made no direct accusation but had proceeded by way of insinuation because he could not prove his charges. The leader of the opposition repeats three times that there was no evidence of corruption. He says:
I do not charge anything in the way of corruption now. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) quoted from page 51 of the report, where Mr. Justice Davis eliminated anything in the way of any suspicion of corruption. I accept that; far be it from me to suggest anything to the contrary.
Why then do they argue if they cannot prove corruption?
But, sir, there are fifty-two pages in this report and I venture to say that on at least forty of them there is an absolute condemnation of the minister and, through him, of the government for having made this contract at all.
I have the report in my hand. This is the report submitted by Commissioner Davis. It is an edition which was printed by Mr. COMMONS
Bren Gun-Mr. Pouliot
Patenaude, printer to the king's most excellent majesty. I recognize it as the only report given by Commissioner Davis; I do not accept as Commissioner Davis's report the other edition which has been compiled with amendments by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. He was not a commissioner in this matter, and he has no right to put any words into the mouth of Commissioner Davis. But he does. I think it is clear what Commissioner Davis had in the back of his mind in speaking as he did at page 703. It is not expressed in the booklet, but one needs very little imagination to understand what he is pointing to. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has a quality that his immediate predecessor never had-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Imagination.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Oh, no; much more than that. His illustrious predecessor was full of imagination, he had too much sail for the rudder; but the present leader of the opposition has a quality which he shares with sheiks of Arabia-he is a mind reader. I suggest to him that he read the mind of his colleagues, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), and even the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart), who is sitting next to him. In the mind of my hon. friend the dean of this house he will find wisdom, but not in the minds of all the other hon. members who support him in the house.
Now, sir, you must consider two things in this discussion. You must consider in the first place this blue book, which is the report made by Commissioner Davis, and which speaks for itself; and in the second place you must consider the very same report which has been transformed into Tory propaganda by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and all his satellites. Therefore I shall not attach much importance to the propaganda booklet. I am more interested in what my hon. friend said when he was speaking for himself than in his interpretation of the opinion given by the commissioner. In fact he did not interpret it; he made it. I would ask the Prime Minister if there was only one commissioner, Mr. Justice Davis, or if there were two, Mr. Justice Davis and the leader of the opposition; and if so, when was the leader of the opposition sworn as commissioner in this case? If he was a commissioner, why did he not present his report with that of Judge Davis? It would not be precisely a minority report; it would be a most 
extraordinary report, a report to the effect that Judge Davis is at the same time right and wrong. He is right when he says there is nothing dishonest; that he says under his own name. But watch the back of his head. The trouble is all there; it is the old saying, nella coda sta il veleno-in the tail the poison.
According to the Financial Post there is mounting opinion on the Bren gun contract. We have received reprints of editorials from newspapers across Canada. But it is easy to provide "mounting opinion." Once I attended a meeting, and the gentleman who had to speak had nothing to say. Pointing to his opponent he said: "Look at that gentleman! Ladies and gentlemen, you know what he has done; you yourselves have never done it, your children have never done it, but he has done it. Why did you not do it? Because you did not feel like doing it, but he felt like doing it and he should be blamed very severely for that." What had he done? Nothing. And public opinion was so much aroused against that man that he could not speak in reply. Well, that is the way Colonel Drew was speaking, before he quit. And that is the way my hon. friends on the other side of the house are speaking now.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has a strong objection on one point mostly- he will correct me if I quote him inaccurately. He said: The curse of democracy is patronage. My hon. friend is strongly against patronage. He made a strong case yesterday, a very strong case. He said, as reported at page 657 of Hansard:
My submission is that the whole report is one of political patronage in its worst form, favouritism to one man, Major Hahn; injustice to other industrialists far more capable and fully equipped-which Major Hahn was not; deception of the Prime Minister in the letter from the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plax-ton) -
It was a kind of deception which was not dishonest, according to Commissioner Davis, but it was deceit just the same.
-of the interdepartmental committee by the various statements made to it by officers in authority; of the British government; and of the people of Canada. Has the Prime Minister -I ask this in all sincerity-read the report completely?
Anyone who knows the Prime Minister would know that he had read the report from the first line to the last.
Frankly it seems to me impossible that he could have read the report and not have condemned the whole deal.
There is a very good reason for that; it is that he read the report and did not see into the back of the head of Commissioner Davis.

Bren Gun-Mr. Pouliot
There is another thing that is most interesting. My hoh. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) said:
Where is the patronage?
Mr. Manion:	Does the minister suggest that
he does not know where the patronage is?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver): I defy my hon. friend to prove it. I defy my hon. friend to prove any patronage.
Why did the Minister of National Defence show so much annoyance about it? If it was patronage, patronage is not so bad after all. Patronage is the rewarding of friends who have fought for us in political campaigns. And when it is within the law there is no need to be scandalized about it. I remember that one who was guilty of patronage, who gave jobs to forty-seven or fifty-seven of his relatives, was my very dear friend the former premier of Quebec, Mr. Taschereau. Once I received a telephone call from the Minister of Justice asking me to speak at Quebec, at the Arena. It was a huge meeting, ten thousand people were there, the meeting was broadcast; it was in the midst of the provincial election campaign of 1931. Everyone I saw-I had to see the barber in the hotel, I was driven to the Arena in a taxi-was speaking about Taschereau having so many relatives employed in the provincial government. They said, "it is shameful." I said, " It is pretty bad." And I went to the meeting to defend the Taschereau candidate. I said: You say Taschereau is guilty of nepotism. It is true. But others are worse. He has forty-seven or fifty-seven relatives in the employ of the provincial government. That sounds very bad; but I know of one who was actually prime minister of Canada and who gave his brother-in-law a job that meant more in the way of financial return than all the Taschereau family together wio-uld receive. And at the time of the appointment of Mr. Herridge my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) was supporting Mr. Bennett, together with the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart); my dear friend the dean of this house, the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. White), the various members for Toronto, the whip of the Conservative party, dear Davenport and Greenwood and Vancouver. They were all supporting Mr. Bennett and they found nothing bad in that. Moreover I was just about to speak during a very important debate when Mr. Bennett in the most tragic voice, like Father Barrett of the Barretts of Wimpole Street, said, "We must adjourn. I have to go to the hospital." He was going to the hospital to see poor dear Mr. Herridge, and strangely enough the fact that Mr. Bennett went there cured Mr. Herridge immediately, so that now both gentlemen can make speeches three times a day. But Mr. Bennett had to adjourn the debate in order to go to see his brother-in-law in the hospital.
Just here I should like to refer to what Lady Beaconsfield did on one occasion. She had accompanied her husband to the House of Commons at Westminster where he was to deliver a most important speech, and on arriving there caught her finger in the door of the carriage but did not say anything because she did not want to disturb him before he made his address. But instead of quoting history let us come back to patronage. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition made a distinction between patronage at large and patronage with regard to the manufacture of munitions, and in that I think he was right. At page 658 of Hansard he said:
I can understand a certain amount of patronage in other matters, but not in munitions. I do object to one man in all this country being chosen, while other industrial people are ignored, and given a contract totalling several millions of dollars.
Well, patronage is the same thing whether it has to do with munitions or anything else, according to the argument of my hon. friend, but he says it is worse in regard to munitions. Why? It is exactly the same thing, according to his own argument. He must remember that the Union government which he supported was most extravagant in regard to munitions. May I recall to him Miss McAdam's life saver with a hole in it? It was a marvellous shield, a shovel with a hole in it, and an enormous quantity was bought by the Union government, just to encourage Sam Hughes' secretary. And the leader of the opposition knows very well that the burden that is so heavy on our shoulders to-day is the war debt. The government he supported at that time may have used one-third of that tremendous amount of money, totalling more than two billion dollars, for real war purposes; one-third was wasted, while the other third was stolen by bandits and gangsters. He knows that, but nevertheless he supported that government.

speechtext:
I am sony to interrupt my hon. friend but I should like to keep the record straight. I do not know anything about the matter he mentioned a moment ago, but since the hon. gentleman says so I presume it is correct, because I have great confidence in him. But I was at the front when the government was carrying on the war, and I was not supporting any government until 1918.
Bren Gun-Mr. Pouliot

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for what he has just said, but coming back from the front in Europe he should have been in the front in Canada to fight such a rotten government.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: You did not go across.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Each in turn. Now, if my memory serves me aright, in 1934 the present leader of the opposition was Minister of Railways and Canals. The hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), who was also in the house at that time, spoke about patronage, and the leader of the opposition had to defend his own position. Here is what he said about patronage, and it is as sweet as milk and honey:
I admit frankly, however, generally speaking, that so far as the appointment of workers on works of my department in the city of Ottawa or elsewhere is concerned, we very frequently do accept the recommendations of the Conservative committee. What is the use of implying anything else, because everybody knows, as the Minister of Public Works has pointed out, that the same charge was made from our side of the house against the last government?
That was on February 16, 1934, and appears at page 651 of Hansard for that year. My hon. friend is like me; he is always sincere and honest, and he went on:
I say quite honestly and quite sincerely that there is no difference, generally speaking, between the system which obtains under this government and that which obtained under the previous one. Not only that, but I believe generally speaking there is a good deal to be said in defence of the practice. I do not mean to suggest that when a man is destitute he should not be given consideration; many of them are. Irrespective of a committee in this city I have on a number of occasions given positions to men who, it was represented to me, were in destitute circumstances.
I pay tribute to his good heart on those occasions, but this reminds me of the overture to a famous opera, I think it is Tann-hauser. I am not sure about that, because I am not strong on music, but I remember how the voices of good and evil are heard at the same time. My hon. friend heard the voice of good that was in his own conscience and his Own heart, but at the same time he was listening to the voices of those around him who were seeking patronage. Then, as he defined it at page 658 of Hansard for yesterday, patronage consists of choosing one man in this country while other industrial people are ignored, giving this man contracts totalling several millions of dollars. I will not say that he has always given contracts involving such sums, but I should like to mention here one instance out of thousands that could be mentioned. My hon. friend remembers when 
his leader, the lamented Mr. Bennett, gave a contract to the Foundation. Company for 82,000,000 at Saint John, New Brunswick, without calling for tenders. I hope if the public accounts committee investigates the Bren gun contract it will get down to real business and investigate the awarding of that contract as well. That is one case; I could give others. Then I quote again from page 651 of Hansard for 1934:
That often occurs, I have not any doubt, in the Department of Public Works, my own department and in others. But, generally speaking-
Mark this.
-generally speaking, it is obvious that the government in power, whether it be Liberal, Conservative or even a government of my hon. friends in the corner-when, a thousand years from now, they gain power-will probably do likewise. It will naturally give consideration to its friends. I do not think any just criticism can be levelled at that.
This is for patronage. But there is something more, Mr. Speaker-something that astounded me. We have discussed-not I, but hon. members opposite-the Bren contract, without ever seeing it. That is incredible. In fact several members from both sides of the house spoke yesterday and I shall deal with them in turn afterwards. At page 695 of Hansard I see the following:
Mr. Stewart: Mr. Speaker, might I ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence to lay on the table a copy of the Bren gun contract?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver): That was done on June 29 of last year, but if the clerk is not seized of it I would be most happy to get a copy or two for my hon. friend.
At noon to-day I phoned downstairs to get that very contract, and I was told that it had been gone for half an hour. Therefore all the hon. members who spoke on the Bren contract never read it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I take the word of the hon. member, but I wonder if he stayed long enough after the session to study it. And besides that, he is not a lawyer, and he has no authority to discuss the legal side of any contract-although he will.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then my hon. friend has no right to discuss the engineering.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

The hon. member has just made the statement that no one had read the contract. I say it is not right that all the hon. members who have spoken in the debate should be charged with not having read the contract. It was open to all of us; it was available to all.

Bren Oun-Mr. Pouliot

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was open to all hon. members, but it was locked in that room downstairs, according to the statement I had at twelve o'clock to-day. No one got it until eleven-thirty. Who got it I do not know. But perhaps they are mind readers and can read a contract that is in a steel locker.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

Mr. Speaker, if I am
allowed by the house to give an expression of my views, may I say that most hon. members confuse points of order and questions of privilege. maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A minute ago the hon.
member for Temiscouata referred to the hon. members .for Winnipeg North Centre and Vancouver North, saying that these two hon. gentlemen were the only ones who spoke yesterday who had read the contract. I demand that that statement be withdrawn.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

When the hon. member

Bren Gun-Mr. Pouliot

The hon. member for

Mr. Speaker, I am quite
prepared to accept the statement-in fact I am prepared to thank the hon. member for Temiscouata for insinuating that I have already won my case.

By leave of the house,
may I finish?

What

We were not given leave

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

When a misconstruction
of fact is made, he has a right to interrupt.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
You need a laugh once in a while yourself.
Mr. DOUGLAS (Weybum),:	As the
seconder of the motion to refer the matter to the public accounts committee-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: And which you voted against.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-and as a member of the public accounts committee

I wish first of all to take issue with the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) last Friday when he stated, in effect, that members who expressed themselves in this debate might possibly preclude themselves from being members of the public accounts committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: He did not say that.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is in
fact what it meant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, it is not.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would like to point out that at least in the last two or three years that has not been the practice. Questions have been referred to standing committees of this house after being discussed pro and con and after hon. members have expressed very definite opinions thereon. A resolution was moved in 1936 with reference to the high price of farm machinery. It was referred to the agriculture committee despite the fact that some hon. members had expressed themselves thereon. Last year and the year before a private bill having to do with small loan companies was referred to the banking and commerce committee after very strong and violent opinions had been expressed on both sides of the house. I think it should be made clear that the committee to which this matter is to be referred is not a judicial body. It is a committee of this house set up for the purpose of investigating, in this case, a contract, and to see whether or not the public interest has been properly guaranteed and the money of the taxpayers properly spent.
Last night the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated that the members of this group had voted against increased defence estimates in 1936, 1937 and 1938, and he went on to say:
Every one of these hon. members was against the expenditure of even the relatively small amount of money that was being proposed at that time. Then what was the position taken when we came to the house in 1937 and asked for 837,000,000? The attitude was exactly the same.
May I point out to the Minister of Agriculture that the members of this group stated then, and they have stated oftentimes since, that the reason they could not and would not vote for increased defence estimates was, first, that they wanted a statement of the government's foreign policy in connection with which these defence estimates would be used and, second, that they wanted a guarantee that the very things which have come to light as a result of this Bren gun inquiry would not occur in Canada. In my

Bren Gun-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
opinion the whole Bren gun inquiry is the best vindication of our consistent opposition in this house to increased defence estimates.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is why you are asking for the investigation?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I turn to the report itself. In my opinion the full intent and purport of this report has never been appreciated. When it first came out headlines appeared in many of the newspapers. For instance, the Montreal Gazette of January 14 contained these headlines:
Bren gun contract held valid; full exoneration is given Mackenzie and Lafleche.
All charges fail.
Davis report clears everyone concerned in affair.
Ottawa is gratified.
Headlines such as these are misleading. In the first place no decision was possible with reference to the actual contract itself. I refer to page 49 of the report on which the commissioner is reported as saying:
I am unable to pass upon the substance as distinct from the form of the contract.
What the house is mainly concerned with) and what the public accounts committee will be concerned with is not whether the contract was technically legal but whether the substance of it was such as to safeguard the interests of the Canadian people. As the commissioner says:
That is a question upon which the government and parliament, in the light of the evidence brought before the commission, must pass.
The commissioner had no power to pass upon the substance of that contract; he could pass only upon its form. As has been pointed out by other hon. members-I am not going to quote this report to death-from pages 31 to 34 will be found argument in which counsel pointed out to the commissioner that he had no jurisdiction to find misconduct because no charge of misconduct had been laid. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was speaking the other day he referred at some length to the wide terms of the reference, and yet I find this at page 33 of the report:
At the noon adjournment the next day government counsel stated that they were afraid that there was not very much that they could contribute in a way of a concrete suggestion, because after all it is a very general and very indefinite subject, having regard to the terms of the order in council.
As was pointed out by one counsel, I believe Mr. Hellmuth, usually when a royal commission is set up there is provision for suggestions with regard to future conduct, but there were no such provisions in the terms of 71492-455
reference in this particular case. May I point out that the Davis commission was a factfinding body. It was not empowered to express opinions. It was not empowered to draw conclusions or to state whether one form of policy was better than another possible alternate form. What the commissioner did was to gather data, assuming throughout that the conclusions to be drawn would be drawn by parliament and by the people of Canada. There are many references to this. For instance, Mr. McRuer is reported on page 32 as having stated to the commissioner:
That is for the House of Commons. You are asked to report the facts, you are asked to report the evidence, and the opinions to be formed will be for the House of Commons, for the people at large, and for the press.
On page 35 I find the same thing. On page 50 I find these words:
The question is: Were proper and sufficient steps taken in this case to discharge that responsibility? Upon the whole evidence, that is a question for the government and parliament to pass upon.
I submit that the statement made when this report was first published that it was a whitewash, that it exonerated everybody, was not well founded. The commissioner did what he was supposed to do. He gathered the data and he left it to this parliament, to this government and to the people of Canada to arrive at conclusions based upon the data which he had collected and verified. He assumed throughout that he was gathering the data so that someone else could formulate a conclusion. Nowhere did he attempt to formulate conclusions with reference to policy and the safeguarding of the interests of the people of Canada.
The Prime Minister said the other day that there might be some people who would think the government was right in refusing a second investigation. I am sure that those who were responsible for moving this motion had no idea of a second investigation being held-not at all. The facts have been collected. Yesterday the leader of the opposition said that there was no value in threshing over old straw and calling witnesses again. Nothing was farther from our minds. The data are there; I believe there are some thirty-four volumes of evidence. The material is at hand, but at the present time there is no one empowered to draw conclusions or pass opinions on it. That is why we are asking that the matter be referred to the public accounts committee. We believe that in such a committee conclusions may be drawn and opinions expressed as to whether or not the public interests of the people of Canada have been properly safeguarded.

Bren Gun-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
Referring to certain speakers who had preceded him, the Minister of Agriculture made this statement, to be found at page 679 of Hansard:
They have left inferences with regard to what the contract may have in it; but I repeat that no one has risen in his place and_ told us what the terms of the contract to which they take such serious objection are.
I propose to deal with only one phase of this contract-although there are many others to which we take serious objection

namely that the giving of this contract was a departure from declared policy in two particulars. I shall deal with them in order.
First, why was there a departure from the declared government policy of manufacturing munitions in government-owned plants? Hon. members will remember that the report points out on page 5 that the original agreement between the Dominion of Canada and the patentee provided that
-such manufacture shall be in a factory operated by the government in question.
That was not done. Why was it not done? It is part of government policy, because on page 10 of the report the Minister of National Defence makes that perfectly clear. I quote:
Under examination by Mr. Hellmuth the Minister of National Defence said that he had stated in the House of Commons last year (1937) that he believed in public ownership, personally, through and through in regard to armaments; "and I still say so." Mr. Hellmuth proceeded with some questions
The answers to which I shall not bother reading, but will summarize by saying that in them the minister reiterates the view that he is in favour of the manufacture of munitions and guns in government plants.
The minister gives two reasons why there was a departure from this policy, and again I quote from page 10:
Q. So that there will be no inducement for people to make money out of necessities which arise from war?
A. Mr. Hellmuth, as a matter of an ideal objective, I completely agree with you; but you should read carefully the recommendations made by a distinguished committee to us early in 1937, in regard to ways of dealing with practical necessities of the Department of National Defence.
And the minister goes on to say:
You should read that.
That was the first reason given by the minister. I should like to refer the members to that report made to the minister in 1937. I have here a summary of it as it appears on page 2288 of the evidence. It was a committee that was set up under the chairmanship of Doctor Skelton. It was an interdepartmental committee, but we will call it

the Skelton committee in order not to confuse it with another-the other-interdepartmental committee that was set up later on. The minutes of this committee were read into the records of the commission. They begin by saying that in 1937 a resolution had appeared on the order paper of the House of Commons-the resolution happened to be my own-calling for, in the event of war, the conscription of the economic, transportation and natural resources of Canada for the duration of the war. In the minutes the committee go on to say that there is a growing opinion in Canada that steps should be taken to take the profits out of war and out of preparation for war, and in view of that the committee made a number of concrete proposals. I shall not give them all, but I should like to read one or two.
Proposal No. 6 was this:
One proposal ... to place manufacture of arms entirely in hands of state . . . the committee is unable to support such a proposal as being practicable under present conditions in Canada but there might be a case for some moderate extension of present government arsenals.
Thqn proposal No. 7:
The committee considered whether new legislation to control private profits might be attempted at this juncture, but they feel unable to suggest any specific legislative measures . . . which could be regarded as workable or effective.
In proposal No. 8 they say that the problem is an administrative one and that:
Control of profits and prevention of excesses can be most efficiently provided by appropriate administrative practice on the part of departments responsible for placing contracts and orders in defence program.
In proposal No. 9 they say that there is no hard and fast rule; that sound financial principles are proper safeguards. In proposal No. 13 are given a number of suggestions which Mr. Elliott, the income tax commissioner, had been asked to draw up, based on the experience that had been gathered during the last war. Mr. Elliott made a number of suggestions and submitted a report, and I just want to draw the attention of the house to one or two of his suggestions. One was that there should be caution to see that "share capital be not inflated by goodwill and other intangible values-that is, make certain that the value behind the share is cash or an asset having real value and paid for in cash or kind of equivalent value." He suggested also that there should be caution as regards salaries paid to executives and shareholders. Certainly these last two suggestions of Mr. Elliott have not been very closely followed.

Bren Gun-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
I come back now to the minister's reasons. The minister says that his first reason for departing from declared government policy was the report of this committee. But this committee said that there might be room "for a moderate extension of government-owned arsenals." That was not done. Why was it not done?
The minister moves on to his second reason. He says that there were two schools of opinion in the department. He says that the chief of the general staff, General Ashton, and the former chief of the general staff, General McNaughton, had both been in favour of the manufacture of arms in government-owned arsenals, but there was another school of thought in the department that was headed by the deputy minister of national defence, which was opposed to the other. I want to quote just one sentence from a letter of the deputy minister of national defence to the under-secretary of state for external affairs. He says:
An arrangement by which the government would take over such a plant and operate the same with its own employees as if it was a government-owned plant does not particularly commend itself to the government.
Here you have in the department two points of view. You have an interdepartmental committee saying that the government-owned plant could extend on a moderate scale, and two high officers of the department, General Ashton and General McNaughton, both favouring that, and the minister pledged to it so far as his declared policy in this house is concerned; and you have the deputy minister opposed to it.
But the minister says the main reason was that they did not have any money. I read now from the bottom of page 10 of the report :
The minister said that General Ashton (the then chief of the general staff) was very insistent upon the development of government arsenals, and that the former chief of general staff, General McNaughton, evolved a very comprehensive scheme for Valcartier, which would include practically all the requirements of the Canadian forces.
Then the report goes on to quote the minister :
That was considered after I went into the department, and I found that the cost of it would be something between $30,000,000 and $35,000,000. With my meagre $25,000,000 or $30,000,000, what could I do with a scheme like that?
Then this is what the commissioner said:
But the testimony given before the commission established that only 60,000 square feet of space was necessary for the purpose of production of the 7,000 Bren guns for Canada as weli as 5,000 guns for the -war office and that an entire new building (apart from land)
would cost approximately $120,000. In proposal "B" of Major Hahn (exhibit 11) of December 29, 1936, the building was shown at an estimated cost of $104,196.40.
I submit that on the minister's own evidence, both as to the report from the Skelton committee and as to the expense involved, we have not had any satisfactory explanation why the government's declared policy of manufacturing munitions and arms in government-owned plants was not carried out.
I move to the second departure from policy. Why was there a departure from the government's declared policy of competitive bidding? In the case of the Bren contract there was, first of all, favoured treatment of one manufacturer and one company. That goes almost without saying. One individual, on the basis of a letter of introduction from a member of this house, was brought into contact with the minister and the deputy minister of national defence, was given first of all snapshots of a gun supposed to be secret and allowed to take it for examination, and was later given a letter to bring him into closer contact with the British authorities. I have no quarrel with that, but when that letter of introduction was not sufficient for him to get the contacts he required he was made a representative of the Canadian government; and from that time on it is very difficult to determine when he is a private contractor seeking a contract and when he is a government representative. It is a sort of "off again on again gone again Finnegan" combination. The most amazing thing of all is that favouritism was shown to the extent that this person -I do not know him personally and I do not cast aspersions upon him; I am dealing with the government, because they are the responsible parties-who was given preferred and favoured treatment throughout, submits expense accounts for work done which in the main was being done in order to procure contracts for himself and the firm of which he was president.
At page 2200 of the evidence I find that there were vouchers of claims up to 820,000 submitted by the John Inglis Company. On October 9. 1936 there is an item of $79.95 and a charge for Major Hahn of $50. This question is put to the deputy minister:
Q. Is this the same day on which Major Hahn called at your office and saw the Bren gun set up?
A. Yes.
Here we have an account for a man calling at the office of the deputy minister to get an entree into the munitions business. An account was submitted 1 In the same evidence, under exhibit 262, there is a charge

Bren Gun-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
of $326.80 between March 14 and March 18, 1938, account rendered for expenses incurred while being at Ottawa to get a contract out of which he was to make a living.
I submit that any group of fair-minded people would say that this was preferred and favoured treatment. No one else in Canada in that business got treatment like that. And may I point out that there was no bidding. No one else was informed that the government intended to go into the manufacturing of Bren machine guns. I refer the house to page 29 of the report. The Minister of National Defence is being questioned by Mr. Hellmuth. I quote:
Q. There was never the slightest etfort, was there, to interest or invite any of these firms to tender, or to make an offer to manufacture the Bren gun?
A. No, I do not think there was.
No one was informed; and yet we find on page 8 this question put by Mr. Hellmuth:
Q. You did not give anybody else a chance?
A. Nobody asked for it.
Well, no one could ask for a chance when no one knew that the government had in mind the manufacture of these guns, according to the minister's own statement. I wonder if the minister honestly meant a statement like that, that nobody had asked for a chance. Are we to assume that from now on all companies in Canada who have facilities for manufacturing munitions are to come once a month or once a week or every day, up to this house and to ask, "Are you manufacturing Bren guns to-day?" Is it to be a sort of Fuller brush pedlar idea? Nobody asked for it! They could not ask when the government had not announced their intention of manufacturing these guns.
It is sometimes said that no one else could make these guns. That was said so often that finally the commissioner began to lose his patience, and on page 1949 of the evidence he said. "Don't be talking to me about one source of supply. I do not want to hear it again. It is ridiculous." Of course it was ridiculous.
I might point-out that the objections I am stating to the fact that there was no bidding did not come only from outside the government. There were serious objections among the officials comprising the interdepartmental committee set up by the Prime Minister to investigate the matter. I refer now to the evidence at page 1948. This is from the minutes of the interdepartmental committee set up to act in conjunction with the depart-
ment of National Defence in giving munitions contracts, and this is what the deputy minister of finance had to say. I am quoting from page 1948:
Doctor Clark then stated that his only objection to entering into a contract with the John Inglis Company was the fact that competitive tendering had not been entered into by three or four other companies capable of manufacturing guns, explaining that he could not, as a member of the committee, take responsibility for the way in which this particular company was selected.
That is pretty strong language. The deputy minister of finance, Doctor Clark, one of the ablest economists in Canada, said that he could not take responsibility for the manner in which this business was being handled because there was no competitive bidding. Now I submit that the government have a right to tell us, and to tell the public accounts committee, why no tenders were called for. We have a right to know whether the situation was carefully canvassed with reference to all outside manufacturers of munitions, in order to ensure that the taxpayers were getting full value for their money. We have a right to know why an objection made by perhaps the ablest business man on the interdepartmental committee was overruled and ignored. We have a right to that knowledge.
I wish to call the attention of the house to this fact, with reference to the officials concerned on the interdepartmental committee, that on two scores their desires and their opinions were either ignored or overruled. As I have said, the committee is on record as in favour of a somewhat moderate extension of the present government arsenals. I refer the house to page 2288. General McNaughton and General Ashton were in favour of it. The government is on record in this house as being in favour of it, and the only person on record as not in favour of the manufacturing of guns in government plants is the deputy minister of national defence. And yet, in spite of that, there was no attempt to carry out the declared policy of manufacturing in government-owned plants.
The officials on the interdepartmental committee were in favour of competitive bidding. They could see no reason why the Inglis company should receive preferred treatment.
I quote from page 37 of the report, where there is a reference to the testimony of Mr. Elliott:
Mr. Elliott, in giving his testimony, said that after the chairman (the deputy minister) had opened the meeting with a general statement indicating the purposes for which the meeting was called the committee began to take an active part in the sense of asking

Bren Gun-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
questions, and getting to grips with the problem. In so doing the committee indicated that competitive bids should be one of the main considerations, and one of the first considerations.	,
And the deputy minister explained that this could not be done. Why? Again I quote Mr. Elliott, page 39. He said that-
-in discussing the financial status of the company, the history of the John Inglis Company was adequately disclosed to the chairman-[DOT]
That is the deputy minister.

namely, the essential point being that it was known that it had been in receivership.
Mr. Elliott continued:
The chairman indicated that he had an understanding-exactly how it was acquired I do not know-from England, that they would not deal with any other firm.
Pressed as to exactly what was said, Mr. Elliott put it this way:
I said as a statement of fact that the chairman stated to us that he believed, or he was of the opinion, whichever way you wish to put it-he believed that England would not place the contract with any other company in Canada.
That was a serious statement. The interdepartmental committee were apparently not very well satisfied.
Mr. Elliott said that the suggestion was then made that a cable be sent to England to ascertain definitely England's position in respect of competitive bids.
The chairman pointed out that to ask such a question at this juncture might endanger the placing of the British order, and endanger thereby the loss which he obviously was anxious to save Canada in the cost of_ the machinery and equipment. The committee nevertheless did not take such notice of that opinion as to withdraw their desire to have the cable sent. They were willing to risk the danger. The form of the cable was then drafted.
The deputy minister (but not without the subsequent approval of the committee) amended their draft cable before it was sent (exhibit 188). Moreover, the deputy minister sent a very long cable himself at the same time to the war office.
In order to keep the record straight I want to say something about these cables. I have copies of them here. I have the cable that was sent by the interdepartmental committee after it had been altered by the deputy minister, of course with the sanction and approval of the committee. It is found at page 1578 of the evidence. It is as follows: Kindly advise by cable production cost in England' of Bren light machine gun specifying which major cost factors have been taken into account and given percentage of each cost factor to the whole. Also the production schedule to which the figures apply. If exact figures are not available close approximation would be much appreciated. This suggestion
on agenda discussed to-day by interdepartmental committee when advisability of obtaining tenders on cost plus basis from limited number of selected companies including John Inglis Company was considered. It is private and not public tender that is intended. The committee would like to know if this would affect the placing of your order in Canada realizing the probable delay incurred thereby. _ This information is for confidential use . . . interdepartmental committee which is working on proposed contract.
I would draw the attention of the house to the words that were inserted at the instance of the deputy minister of national defence: "from limited number of selected companies including John Inglis Company"; also: "It is private and not public tender that is intended."
I have here the reply of the war office and also the private cable sent by the deputy minister of national defence to the war office to explain the one that had been sent by the interdepartmental committee. And I have the reply that came back to the deputy minister from the war office. My time is getting short, so perhaps I cannot read it, but after very carefully reading these cables from beginning to end I defy any hon. member to find any indication that the war office stated at any time that they were not willing to deal with any company other than the John Inglis Company.
On the basis of that statement and of his insistence the deputy minister either ignored or overruled the two wishes expressed by the interdepartmental committee; one for a moderate extension of government-owned arsenals, and the other for the principle of competitive bidding.
What was done about this other statement of Doctor Clark? I quote from page 1949 of the evidence:
The Chairman-
That is, the deputy minister.
___reminded the members that on a previous
occasion the precise question came up as to whose responsibility it was for picking a likely firm to manufacture the gun, and at that time, some six months ago, he told the committee that his department would have to take the responsibility.
At page 1952, in reference to Doctor Clark, the minutes say:
He stated that he wished it understood by the public and the government that the committee had reviewed the financial aspects of contracts such as this, and considered them fair and reasonable-
I am quoting now the statement of Doctor Clark.
-but in this contract he stated that he would not say that they are.

Bren Gun-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
And what happened? The chairman, that is the deputy minister of national defence-[DOT]
then explained that the wording of the report to council was not such as to involve the members of the committee in matters of choice. . . .
What was this committe set up for? When they had finally come to certain conclusions and the deputy minister of finance said he would not accept responsibility for this method of selection, that he did not think it a good business arrangement, the deputy minister of national defence overruled him and said that his department would have to accept the responsibility and that the members of the interdepartmental committee had no power of choice. What power had they?
One thing more. Was any report ever made by this interdepartmental committee to the government? I have here in the evidence the statement made by the Minister of National Defence himself, as found at page 2364, where he says:
The only report I ever received was from the deputy minister who was chairman of the interdepartmental committee.
And that was a verbal report. He never had a brief from the committee. That interdepartmental committee was set up by the government to safeguard the interests of the people of Canada. Did the Prime Minister ever get a report? Did the Minister of Finance ever get a report? No. But his deputy minister had objected to this contract as an unbusinesslike arrangement. Did other members of the cabinet know that perhaps the finest financial mind among the government's officials objected to this method of selecting the company? Of course they did not. I doubt if the Minister of National Defence himself knew it; all he knew about was the verbal report given to him by the chairman of the committee, the deputy minister of national defence, who throughout the sittings of this committee had ignored and overruled the opinions expressed by members of that committee.
