speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I have to inform him that his time has expired.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We are discussing a motion by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) to refer what is known as the Bren gun agreement to the standing committee on public accounts. It will be noticed that no instructions are included in this motion. I propose, before I take my seat, to suggest an amendment which I hope will be acceptable to the house. What I shall say this afternoon will TMr. T. C. Douglas.]
be uttered in as dispassionate a manner as possible. I should like to discuss the question frankly and in a way to appeal to the good judgment of the government themselves and hon. members of the house. Obviously I cannot cover all the ground, or any very large portion of it, in the time available to me; so I am not contending that my argument to-day will be a complete argument of the case. I should like to base what I have to say upon a paragraph which will be found on page 50 of the report of the royal commission on the Bren gun contract, and which has already been referred to by a number of speakers. There, referring to the question whether an article should be manufactured by the government or by private interests, the learned judge says:
. . . the heaviest sort of responsibility falls upon those charged with the duty of selecting the individual, firm or corporation to manufacture the article. The question is: Were proper and sufficient steps taken in this case to discharge that responsibility? Upon the whole evidence, that is a question for the government and parliament to pass upon.
As far as I am concerned as a member of this house I accept my own responsibility to review this situation, as advised or suggested by the learned judge who presided over that commission.
Before discussing the contract, which I propose to do, I should like to make a brief reference to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), that in submitting the reference to Mr. Justice Davis, the commissioner, he enclosed in his letter a press release; and the right hon. gentleman suggested, as I certainly inferred, that he thought this was quite sufficient. I am not quarreling with him in that regard, Mr. Speaker, but another press release was given out from the Prime Minister's office at the conclusion of the inquiry. That second release was sent throughout the length and breadth of Canada; the general headline based upon the wording of that release was the term "exoneration." w'ith the inference that everything connected with the Bren gun contract had been satisfactorily explained to the commissioner.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I say that my hon. friend is entirely wrong. There was no press release sent out from my office at the end of the inquiry. I want to make that emphatically clear; there was nothing authorized, directly or indirectly. The only statement that went from my office was that the report was in my hands and that no one had seen it.

Bren Gun-Mr. Stevens

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I accept the right hon. gentleman's word unreservedly, but in justice to myself I must say I was told that the dispatch carried by the Canadian Press was handed to them by the private secretary of the Prime Minister. I may be wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is absolutely wrong.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I accept the Prime Minister's statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend and the house that no statement was given by me or any of my secretaries.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It would be interesting, I think, to know where that statement came from. It came from some source associated with the government. The question, however, I was going to ask was:	When that
latter release to the press was given out, wherever it came from, was it first submitted to the learned judge who presided over this commission, in regard to its accuracy or its harmony with his findings? I doubt whether it was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend too often

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have accepted my right hon. friend's explanation without reserve.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The point I want to bring out is this: For myself I could never see that there was any authority for that statement from any source. Such reports as appeared seemed to me to be something that some member of the press itself had sent out, without authority from any source.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I shall check the source of my information, but of course in the meantime I accept the right hon. gentleman's word on the matter without reserve.
Conditions in Canada in regard to defence have been represented as serious, and this year we are asked to vote $63,000,000 for the purpose of defence. What we are doing in this contract is initiating a practice. We are laying the foundation of a practice to be followed in the expenditure of this huge sum of money. If this contract and its method, style, form and nature are now approved and accepted, then we can take it that, in the expenditure of that part of this $63,000,000 which goes to this class of work, the same sort of policy will be followed. Therefore in my opinion it is extremely important that we, the houses of parliament, should be satisfied with the basis on which we are now entering upon a huge expenditure which may 71492-46
be followed in subsequent years by still further expenditures, since this is a ten year-contract.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am coming to that, if my hon. friend will permit me. If that be so, it means that in future years we are going to follow the same practice we are here following. I mention that merely because it emphasizes the importance of this contract.
There are three ways in which we could approach this great, serious task, which on several occasions the right hon. Prime Minister has indicated he considers a very onerous and grave responsibility. There is government production; there is contract by tender, or there is the cost-plus basis with a selected contractor. These are three methods; there may be others that modify them to a certain extent. I want to get to the contract itself; so I am not going to take time just now to argue as to the advisability of public production. Let us assume that we are going to accept the principle of production by private concerns. In that case I submit, and if time permitted I think I could demonstrate fully, that it would be infinitely preferable to place this or similar orders with a number of firms qualified to do the work.
Let me just indicate briefly, by way of illustration, what I mean. I am not a technician, so I may speak rather recklessly in this regard; but I understand that in a gun of this kind there is the tripod, or whatever the thing rests upon; there is the rough frame of the gun, what might be called the stock, and then there is the barrel, which is a comparatively simple article to manufacture. Then somewhere in that gun, as in all weapons of this kind, there are some intricate parts which must be manufactured. There would be no difficulty in giving to certain firms orders for barrels and to other firms orders for tripods or frames. These are simple articles. Of course they must be made right, but there are scores of firms who could manufacture that sort of thing. Then you come to the intricate part, which I am told calls for perhaps fifty, seventy-five or one hundred gauges, the most delicate instruments it is possible to procure. I am told that in some forms of production over a hundred, and perhaps two hundred, gauges may be required for different parts which are of an exceedingly delicate nature.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: More than that; three hundred and ten, if I am not mistaken.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In any case my hon. friend will agree that it is an extremely delicate

Bren Gun-Mr. Stevens

process. Great care should be taken, in dealing with this part of the .work, to select a firm that not only is organized to-day to do this class of work but also has a staff accustomed to it, such as superintendents, foremen of machine shops or portions of machine shops and experts of that kind, of course over and above the experts who understand the complete article. I submit that we might have borrowed from the old country-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have; three of them.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Very good-experts who would advise with those who are competent to carry on this work. But my point is that, with the utmost respect and consideration for the group who secured this contract, it cannot be argued for one moment that they had any organization. They had no organization, whereas on the other hand we might have gone to one of a dozen firms in this country whom I could name, who are engaged in precision tool work of some kind, who have the experts, who, under the leadership of the ordnance experts brought from the old country, could have taken up this matter very quickly and readily, and who have the organization and the nuclei at least of a plant for the purpose.
It is said that this is a good contract. Well, I have read over the contract, and I think it is a good contract-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: -for the contractor.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Too soon.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And I will point out why. In making that statement I am not casting any reflection upon the contractor. His business was through his solicitors, and it is com-lucn knowledge that a man will get the best contract he can. I have read the contract with care, and I believe it is an excellently drawn contract, for the contractor. In some respects of course it protects the interests of the government. That we would expect. But I believe I shall show, before I take my seat, that there are provisions in the contract which are at least questionable-I shall just put it in that way.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who spoke yesterday on behalf of the government, suggested that nothing had been said against this contract by Colonel Drew; that nothing had been said against it before the commission by any witness-in brief that nothing had been said against the contract. I shall suggest a few things-and

the minister invited us to make suggestions- which I think should make us pause before we sanction or place the approval of parliament on the Bren contract.
In the first place it is a contract giving a licence for ten years. The contract states:
The terms of this licence shall be for a period of ten years from the date hereof.
And then it says that the terms of this licence may be renewed or extended for a further period of ten years. It may be argued that the licence is not an exclusive licence- and, by the terms of the contract, that is true. But it would be hard to persuade me, when I read the whole contract, that it is not intended to be what is virtually an exclusive licence. Or, I will go farther:	If
under the terms of the contract the government, as they are bound to do, supply all the machinery for the production of the gun- and those are virtually the terms of the contract-how on earth could anyone else get into the game, after the manufacturing gets under way? How could that be done, unless the government repeats, with a second licencee, the same thing they did for the original licencee? So, whether or not the licence is exclusive in its terms, it is exclusive in its nature, and in the facts surrounding it. That is my first objection.
My second objection lies in the following:
The party of the second part-
That is the company; really it is Major Hahn.
-undertakes and agrees with the party of the first part to manufacture 7,000 of the said Bren gun, as defined in schedule 1.
And then it says:
There will be installed in the buildings made available by the party of the second part the machinery, tools, dies, jigs and gauges necessary for the manufacture of the said Bren gun, in accordance with exhibit A attached and forming part of these presents, it being expressly agreed that the machinery therein mentioned when so installed shall be capable-
Mark these words:
-of being utilized to produce Enfield rifles, pistols and other small arms as well as parts and components thereof.
Obviously the contract contemplates its extension to include the manufacture of articles other than Bren guns, or that language would not be in there.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Not
necessarily.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Again I agree with the
minister. But with an exclusive contract financed by the government of Canada and with machinery supplied by the government of Canada-

Bren Gun-Mr. Stevens

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And
Great Britain.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-surely it is not going
to be suggested that in connection with a company equipped, as they say it must be- it is obligatory on the contractor-to manufacture Enfield rifles and pistols, no one contemplates giving them that work to do. Is the government going to set up another manufacturer, in the same way? Not at all. The minister knows that once the contract was running smoothly-and it would have been, had we not interfered-there would have been an extension of the contract to these other lines.
I may say it was the talk around Ottawa last May and June that this firm was on the way to being a real munitions producer and was going to get other work.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
On a
point 'of order, the minister knows nothing of the kind. There have been no obligations, nor has there been any permission of any kind whatsoever given, with reference to this firm, in regard to any other contract.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Delete that clause from
the contract, then; it is not necessary. Let us delete it. I object to the contract because that clause appears in it.
Then the next point:
As compensation for the said machinery, tools, dies, jigs, gauges-[DOT]
And so on.
-the party of the first part shall pay to the party of the second part an amount computed on a basis of two-thirds of that set out hereunder, of which the said two-thirds shall be payable by the said party of the first part in the manner hereunder set forth-
This point has already been dealt with by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas).
1. A sum not exceeding $20,000, in respect of actual cost of preliminary investigation. . . .
I object to that, and I will point out why. There is not a manufacturing concern in Canada which does not at times come to Ottawa. It is open to any manufacturing concern in Canada to come to Ottawa, as they do by doaens, always paying their own expenses. They consider such expenses out-of-pocket, day-to-day expenditures incidental to business. It is absurd for the taxpayers of this country to be asked to pay S20.000 for "planning and engineering" services, entirely apart from the contract. That is important, and is another of my objections.

speechtext:
Did the
hon. member read the evidence in regard to that?
71492-46J

What

It has

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

speechtext:
There are in the contract many things which I certainly hope were not suggested by the Canadian government.
But let us go on.
2. The actual cost to the party of the second part of such machinery, tools, dies, jigs and gauges as it procures from outside sources.
I am not taking great objections to that, so long as the principle I have indicated is adopted. Then:
The actual cost-
And I am reading this for a purpose.
-to the party of the second part of such machinery, tools, dies, jigs and gauges as it manufactures.
And then comes this:
Such other costs, as are set out in section 5 of this agreement, as are properly chargeable under this contract in the fulfilment by the party of the second part of its obligations up to date of commencement of manufacture of the Bren gun.
That is one of those omnibus clauses which allow a contractor to work in what we commonly call, in government contracts, overages.
71C
Bren Gun-Mr. Stevens

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Not
necessarily.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is the British practice.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not care whether it is the British practice or not; I object to it. Here is another point to which I object:
The party of the first part shall also pay the cost of such conversion of the plant of the party of the second part as is in the opinion of the party of the first part necessary or advisable in making the said plant suitable for the carrying out of the terms of this contract but no such cost shall be repaid to the party of the second part, except such as has been given prior approval by the party of the first part.
It may be argued quite properly that this is a fair clause, but my point is that it was represented that this firm or this group of individuals had a number of plants equipped for this purpose. It was stated in 1936 that there were a number of plants equipped for this purpose, but here in 1938 we are agreeing under a contract to pay all the costs of equipping and converting this plant. I should like to quote from a letter of October 20, 1936, from the deputy minister of national defence to the under secretary of state for external affairs. This letter appears on page 20 of this report, and I quote as follows:
-and representing a reliable group which controls certain manufacturing plants-
Plural.
-capable of manufacturing armaments and munitions located in a large industrial centre.
By no stretch of the imagination can it be said that this plant was capable of manufacturing munitions.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Did they not do it during the last war?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister asks, did we do it in the last war?
fMr. Stevens.]

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, this plant.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does
the hon. member know anything of its
record?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I know the record of the plant and I knew the late Mr. Inglis quite well. It is a splendid company, but it is not equipped for the manufacture of munitions of this kind.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Why
not? Does my hon. friend know anything of the record of this company during the late war?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: They manufactured shells and other kinds of munitions, but they did not manufacture this gun.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: What the hon. member has just read does not mention the Bren gun; it refers only to the manufacture of munitions and armaments.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The people of Canada are to pay the total cost of converting this plant into a munitions plant. I pointed out further that the group which got this contract represented that they had a plant suitable for the manufacture of munitions. The next point to which I object is this:
The party of the first part shall pay the cost of dismantling and moving the same as well as the cost of replacing in its original condition, subject to reasonable wear and tear, such property of the party of the second part as has been originally moved or shifted by reason of the installation in the plant of the party of the second part.
That may be considered a normal clause to have in a contract provided you accept the principle that you are going to take a plant not suitable for manufacturing munitions and convert it at public expense into one suitable for that purpose. If you accept that position then you must accept the position of replacing it in its original condition if the contract is cancelled. But I object to that particular part of the contract. Reference is made to the price of the said Bren gun and spare parts thereof as ordered by the party of the first part, but I cannot cover all this long list. I shall, however, cover a few to which I take exception. One clause reads:
(a) The sum of all costs, as hereinafter defined, properly incurred in connection with the manufacture of the said Bren gun and spare or component parts thereof.
Then the contract enumerates certain exemptions such as sales tax, royalties, licensing fees and, mark you, interest on bank loans. That is covered by paragraph four of subsection (a)

Bren Gun-Mr. Stevens
of section four. Then on page ten of the contract we find a clause dealing with interest on bank loans which reads:
Interest on bank loans raised by the party of the second part for the purpose of providing any additional plant which may be required and approved by the party of the first part.
First, it exempts interest on bank loans, and then this clause is included. I object to the apparent contradiction, not to say deception, in those two clauses. Then it goes on:
It being expressly agreed that the total amount payable under this clause and under section 3 (e)	(5) of this contract shall not
exceed the sum of two hundred and sixty-seven thousand dollars ($267,000) in respect of seven thousand (7,000) guns as defined in schedule 1 attached hereto.
It has been emphasized over and over again that a limitation is placed upon the profits of this company, that limit being put strictly at $267,000. The house will notice a qualifying phrase in section 3 (e) (5). In other words, it exempts from this limitation that section to which I have already referred, namely, section 3 (g) which deals with the cost of dismantling and depreciation, which are exempted. The limitation does not protect the country against additional expenditures in connection with those operations. Here again I object to the form of the contract.
I turn now to later clauses in the contract dealing with depreciation in the value of the buildings. The contract states:
The annual rates of depreciation to be allowed shall be 2J per cent on brick or stone buildings, five per cent on wooden buildings, and ten per cent on machinery, other than on machinery referred to in section 3 hereof.
There is already included in the contract wear and tear brought about by manufacturing the gun. Anyone who knows anything about industrial plants and the setting up of depreciation accounts in the operation of a plant, knows that when a plant is in operation it is maintained. This plant is to be maintained throughout the whole term of the contract at the cost of the people of Canada. Yet in addition to that, depreciation such as I have mentioned, particularly ten per cent on the machinery, is to be allowed. Wear and tear, lubrication and other things are provided for in the contract; we are paying for renewal and maintenance, and in addition we are to pay ten per cent depreciation on machinery.
My time is almost exhausted, and I come now to one point that I desire to make. In the schedule, named exhibit D, we have an extraordinary statement:
Schedule of deliveries from date of execution and delivery of the attached agreement:
24th-36th month inclusive, 1,000 guns-
That is, three years from last March,
1.000 guns; next, four years from last March,
3.000 guns; next, five years from last March,
6.000	guns; and next, five and a half years from last March, 2,000 guns. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we are told that the reason why this contract was made was the pressure of time, the immediate need, the danger, and here we have the first gun coming in three years after the signing of the contract-no, the first 1,000 guns are to be delivered three years after the signing of the contract.
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver:) Will my hon. friend compare that with the record of any other country?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Here are the facts. The minister may in his own mind justify it, but I am questioning it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The statement of the hon. gentleman is inaccurate, and he ought to withdraw it and read the contract. Three years, he said, before the first gun is to be delivered.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I corrected that, and said
1.000	guns to be delivered within the three years.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No; 1,000 to be delivered within twenty-four to thirty-six months. Read the contract.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is three years. I read exactly what is here: 1,000 guns to be delivered twenty-four to thirty-six months after the signing of this contract. Make whatever you like of it.
My time is almost gone, and I should just like to make this observation in the few minutes remaining before I read my amendment.
I think the contract is an improvident one. I want to say this to the Prime Minister: I am not at all disposed to attack the good faith of the minister or his staff; but I do say that the record of the evidence, of the interdepartmental committee, and the observations of the learned judge who drew up that report, must raise in the minds of anyone who will read it grave doubts as to the wisdom of this contract. I have gone through it myself with some care. I have touched hastily on only a few points in connection with it. My opinion is that this contract should be cancelled; we can pay the necessary compensation that might be warranted, and then let us start this big expenditure of $63,000,000 on a sound basis. This contract is the most unfortunate basis from which Canada could possibly launch forth upon an expenditure of $63,000,000.
Bren Gun-Mr. Stevens

One reason why we do not approve of this matter going to the public accounts committee as proposed by the motion, is that there are no instructions given to the committee. The matter simply goes to the public accounts committee, and we all know what happens in committees. It is extremely difficult, with one party having an overwhelming majority on the committee, to get an impartial discussion. This house is the place in which the discussion should take place.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: You are having it now.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We are having it now.
I come now to my amendment, and I am sure the Minister of National Defence will welcome this. We think this amendment is preferable to the motion because it lays on parliament all the responsibility, and we want to say to those who proposed the motion, in perfectly good faith, that while we do not wish the matter to go to the public accounts committee, we shall certainly support the motion for sending it there if all our efforts to get the matter dealt with on the floor of this house are defeated. We want to make that very clear. All the essential facts are before parliament. Everything we can possibly ask for is in the evidence and in the report, and so I now move, Mr. Speaker seconded by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. White):
That all the words after the word "to" in the fourth line thereof be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"The committee of the whole house, with instructions that the committee consider the advisability of cancelling the said contract."
The amendment seems to arouse the mirth of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). Apparently he does not agree with his deputy on this matter. The motion, Mr. Speaker, will then read:
That the agreement for the manufacture of Bren machine guns, the report of the royal commission dealing with said agreement and all related documents, evidence, vouchers and exhibits, be referred to the committee of the whole house with instructions that the committee consider the advisability of cancelling the said contract.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment is properly discharging the responsibility placed upon parliament by the learned judge who presided over the royal commission.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I refrained from participating in the debate on the address, feeling that the wealth of numbers and material from all quarters of the house had made a sufficient contribution to the discussion at that stage; and having so refrained, I desire the house to know that

I expect to be able to represent the views of my riding of Parry Sound from time to time as specific matters come before us.
Not having addressed the house before this session, may I crave its indulgence to digress for one moment to pay a tribute to the hon. leader of his majesty's opposition in this house (Mr. Manion). I have not had the privilege of knowing him intimately for very long, but I may say that he has a personality which has entirely captured me so far as his demeanour, his sense of humour, and all those good qualities we like to find in our fellow-man are concerned. If during the course of my remarks in this debate I find it necessary to criticize his public utterances and conduct and to refer, perhaps shortly, to some doctrine that he has laid down in the book which he wrote for the guidance of the people with regard to the vilification of public men in public office and with regard to other topics that seem to me apropos to this debate, he will understand, I know, that there is nothing personal in what I say but that it is his public utterances and his public desire to instruct the people of Canada with which I quarrel.
We find ourselves, Mr. Speaker, engaged in a serious debate. Being, I find, a member of the public accounts committee, I shall, in reviewing now some phases of this question, endeavour so far as possible not to pass final judgment upon the contract under review, and not to pass final judgment upon the report of the Hon. Mr. Justice Davis, which has been so much-discussed. But I do propose to endeavour to have the members of this house and incidentally the people of Canada, understand the genesis and the raison d'etre of the fuss that has been raised in its various forums and the history with regard to the contract for the manufacture of Bren guns.
I propose to charge the young man who wrote this article with having done so for a purely political, partisan purpose. I propose to take this house, if I may, to a convention room in the Royal York hotel on November 9 and to quote a statement made by the young gentleman in bidding for the leadership of his provincial party, a statement he made with reference to this matter which will stamp him in language that I would refrain from using. I propose then to deal very shortly with the course adopted before the royal commission, and then, if time permits, with the. course adopted by the hon. gentlemen who occupy the front benches opposite, and who have made such eloquent speeches in denunciation of our beloved Minister of National Defence of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie).
Let me first make reference to some pages of what I regard as a most entertaining and

Bren Gun-Mr. Slaght
delightful book. I regret that my hon. friend opposite who wrote it, in addition to his ripe and wide experience in many phases of life, had not had the privilege of spending ten years of his life, as I did of mine, with the miners and prospectors of northern Ontario. If anything could have widened his experience and improved his book it would have been that. An interesting topic which the leader of the opposition purports to deal with for the instruction of his readers is found at pages 271 and 272 where he deals with the vilification of public men. At page 271 he points his thesis by writing of an experience. Let me read what he says:
On one occasion many years ago, while idling in the smoking room of a pullman car, I listened to a conversation in which politicians were roundly condemned for their "grafting and crookedness," the critics not being aware that a member of the house was among them. Getting tired of their criticism X turned to the loudest among them and said.
"I happen to come from Ottawa;-know many members very well-and am convinced that as a class they are as honest as other men. Would you mind telling me upon what you base your statements that members of parliament are grafters and crooks?"	.
"I am sorry, sir," he replied apologetically, "but I have nothing whatever to base them upon. I have heard others say the same thing, and was merely repeating their statements."
Upon such gossip does reputation often founder! It is as unwise as it is unfair that vilification of this kind should be indulged in, certainly unless one can prove his accusation to be true.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is some more wisdom laid down in this same volume. The hon. gentleman has undertaken to tell us what the duty of an opposition in parliament is, and I trust that his extended experience in that capacity may not be cut short too soon. I should like to make a brief reference to what he says in this book. At page 275 I quote:
From 1920 to 1930 we spent four more years in the shades of opposition. It is a freelance life, with plenty of opportunity for criticisms and little real responsibility for the proper carrying on of national affairs, for the party in power makes it a question of honour to have its own way. An active opposition may be of great use to a government and to a country if it uses its powers of criticism in a sane and constructive manner-
I call attention to the next few lines, which contain the nut in the coconut of this debate: . . . but few oppositions worry overmuch about constructive suggestions, aiming rather to point out the blunders of a government, and rarely showing sufficient generosity to praise worthy actions.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I wrote that right after I had observed my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) in opposition for five years

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I take it the hon. gentleman was sincere, after his experience in opposition, when he related what he and his confreres thought wal the duty of an opposition. I do not agree with him and I do not commend his view to the youth of Canada as indicating the duty of an opposition. If he will search the records of British parliamentary life he will find that the best tradition in England dissents entirely from such a statement as that which he has written.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just after the house took recess several hon. members asked me for the name of the book from which I had quoted, which name I inadvertently omitted to state. The name of the book is, "Life is an Adventure;" the author is the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), and it may be procured at any reputable bookshop for the modest price, I understand, of $2.50. I assure my hon. friend I am seeking no part in the royalties.
I stated that this whole Bren gun agitation was, in my view, inspired by purely political motives, and I propose to spend the few minutes at my command in outlining my reasons for making that statement. We had a scholarly and interesting address from the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) just before recess. I disagree with most of what he said, but in these times of war and strife I feel that the house should be congratulated upon the fact that two of the great parties of Canada have found peace and are now under the one banner: the great Reconstruction party and the great Conservative party-the National Conservative party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Formerly the Liberal-Conservative party.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have not always agreed with the hon. member for Kootenay East, but I think it is to his everlasting credit that in this debate he was quick to dissociate himself from his new-found leader in his imaginative and bitter criticism directed against the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). We did get a clue from the speech of the hon. member for Kootenay East as to the inside workings of this Tory cabal to destroy the Minister of National Defence. In the course of his remarks he
Bren Gun-Mr. Slaght

was, as I noted it, referring to the contract, and he said or predicted: "Once this contract is running smoothly, which it would have been had we not interfered," then so and so would follow. There is the clue to the situation, and the disturbance in Canada for the last eight months: "Had we not interfered it would have been running smoothly." No truer word has been uttered in this debate. Notwithstanding the admitted interference, for purely partisan purposes I repeat, the contract has been, to the disappointment of my hon. friends opposite but to the great satisfaction of the people of Great Britain and the British war office, running more than up to date on its commitments.
Let me digress for a moment to refer to the evidence of Mr. Gillespie who was called as a witness. He has been and is in charge of the John Inglis plant for the production of these guns. I refer to page 3091 and following pages of the evidence taken before the commission.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Who is Mr. Gillespie?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am glad to tell the hon. m'ember who Mr. Gillespie is and then to tell him what he says. Mr. Gillespie was for thirty-eight years in the employ of the British war office. He was for eighteen years in charge of the royal small arms factory at Enfield, the greatest munition producing factory in the British empire. He agreed to come to this country and undertake the supervision of this contract in the John Inglis Company's plant for the life of the contract, and the British war office released him to Canada for that purpose. His duties in the royal small arms factoiy at Enfield were-I paraphrase the evidence-to develop the manufacture of all sorts of small arms and machine guns, guns that would take the ordinary rifle cartridge. His evidence discloses that he was sent by the British Ministry of Munitions to the United States, to help them with their difficulties in regard to small arms, and spent some time in various factories there, including the Winchester repeating arms factory at Schenectady, the Remington factory at Ilion, and the Savage company. What does that gentleman say, compared with the slanderous imputations from the other side of the house that this firm and its equipment are not capable of producing the Bren gun as required by the terms of their contract? At page 3106 we find the following, in reference to the Inglis organization:
Q. And from your experience with them here what do you say as to their efficiency as engineers in charge of production, or in charge of planning for production of Bren guns?

A. I would say they are one hundred per cent.
Q. One hundred per cent?
A. Yes.
Q. Well that is pretty good.
The Commissioner: As the school boy says, it is not good, it is perfect.
That is the testimony of a man who is qualified to speak. We have discovered in our midst a young engineer. Let me say that while I disagree with 99 per cent of what he said I think he made a masterly presentation of a bad case, as he is always capable of doing. I have complimented him upon that; I regard him as one of my friends in the house, and I hope I am right in that. But are we to take the speeches of young engineers and of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house who have achieved a great deal in their respective spheres, and throw out the testimony of a man who is preeminent in the manufacture of munitions in the British empire to-day? The people of Canada will not take long to choose.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Did the hon. gentleman
say that Mr. Gillespie is the head of the Inglis company?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, my friend misunderstood me. He is lent to the Inglis company by the British war office.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: But he is in charge of the Inglis company now, do I understand?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, and he was there when they opened the doors and put these workmen to work, and has been there ever since. He was called to testify, and the arrangement is that he stays until this contract is fulfilled.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: And I understand in that evidence he is speaking for a company which he is managing at the present time? I understood the hon. member to say that this gentleman is manager or superintendent or something for the company at the present time; is that right?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, for the John Inglis
Company; that is right.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: So he was speaking of his own company when he said it was so up to date.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, but does my friend suggest that he prevaricated? He speaks with a record of thirty-eight years in the British war office behind him.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Was he engaged before the contract was signed; was that one of the reasons?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order.

Bren Gun-Mr. Slaght

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, I want to answer.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Cooperation with the
British by hon. members on the other side!

speechtext: The hon. member is sure-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

speechtext: Question.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have only one question: Is the hon. member quite positive of what he is saying?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: This interruption has taken three minutes, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Let me answer my hon. friend. I believe, definitely, that I have stated the facts. I have studied the evidence, and I think if my hon. friend has read it-which I very much doubt

he will find that the statement I have made is absolutely correct. We can all make mistakes here and there, but let my hon. friend read the evidence, and then point out the mistake.
That, Mr. Speaker, brings me to a point with which I had not intended to deal here. My hon. friends on the other side of the house, in all their criticism, have failed to tell us one thing. In the friendliest way I challenge the leader of the opposition if he has read the evidence-which I doubt-to tell us what part the British war office took in scrutinizing the contract which they made, which is on all fours with the Canadian contract under attack except as to the quantity of guns and except as to one provision which we put in for the protection of the government of Canada, and which the British war office did not even insist upon. It is all very well for
my hon. friend to say to me, " Oh, you can deal with that." If he wants to present a fair case to the people of Canada, why does he criticize Mr. Orde, who, as I understand it, was a Conservative appointee?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I did not criticize Mr. Orde at all.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Why does he suggest that the experts in Canada, legal, engineering and otherwise, made any error in advising their government to enter into this contract? Does he forget that for long months the British war office, whose experience goes back a hundred years, whose expert engineers and legal counsel I say transcend a hundredfold all the carping criticism that came from the other side, scrutinized a similar contract, which now bears the signature of the British war office and which they desire to have carried out? Why not be fair? Why sit down without dealing with that point when invited to do so? Under his theory of the duty of an opposition does he present the carping criticisms and refuse to acknowledge the good that may lie in the subject under discussion? That is not his exact language, but it is a paraphrase of his conception of the duty of an opposition, and he has demonstrated it to the nth degree in his conduct during this debate.
Now let me get to my real point, Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Thank you-and it is this: From the day the Maclean's article was published it was a plan and scheme conceived in the brain of the young man who wrote it, for what fee has never yet been disclosed- my hon. friend says $500. I do not know. It might have been $500, or it might have been thirty pieces of silver. I am not sure as to which it might have been. But let me tell my hon. friends across the way that from that very day there has been a consistent cabal to close the plant of the John Inglis Company.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will tell us something about fees.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Fees; he knows about fees. What was the fee that the author got? I am asking the hon. gentleman a question. Will he tell me what the fee was for the Maclean's magazine article?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What is the hon. gentleman's question?
Bren Gun-Mr. Slaght

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would the hon. member tell us what was the fee for the article to which he referred?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member knows that now; why is he asking?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, I do not; I am asking for information. We have an hon. gentleman speaking who knows more about fees than all the rest of this House of Commons put together. Tell us about the fee; tell us what, it was.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is not a proper
question.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When my hon. friend finds me accepting a fee to traduce a contract that is on all fours with a contract entered into by the British war office, which means a supply of guns and ammunition for the mother country when she is in dire need, then he can bring in any criticism of me he wishes.
Let us see what George Drew wanted, and I would ask hon. members to notice the date I am about to mention. An interview appeared in the press on September 1, 1938. That interview was with Mr. Dingman of the Globe and Mail staff, appearing in the Globe and Mail of September 2. The heading is:
Drew Demands Work Stopped on Bren Guns.
Would Close Inglis Plant till Probe of Deal is Concluded.
That is a significant date, September 1. A reference to the report of the commission will show that the report was brought in on December 29. If George Drew had had his way the Inglis plant would have been closed down for three months and twenty-seven days so that a young politician might become leader of his provincial party. Will any hon. gentleman across the way dare state, now or later, that he approves such a demand? The question answers itself; no. Did Colonel Drew consult the British war office as to what effect it might have on their plans if the Inglis plant were closed for four months? Certainly not.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It could be closed for
four years and make no difference.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend has now allied himself, as I hoped he would not, with an attempt to close the Inglis plant when the British war office had urged that the work be carried on. This young gentleman did not stop at that. We all know of the two months during which the inquiry proceeded, in which he took a prominent part as counsel. We know that he is a member of the bar of Ontario, and we know that members of the bar, both

British and Canadian, have a clear understanding that matters sub judice, as it is said in law, or matters which have not been finally dealt with by a tribunal before which evidence has been presented, should not be discussed in public, certainly not by a counsel engaged in the case and certainly not by a quasi litigant or accuser.
Let me take you, Mr. Speaker, to that historic room in the Royal York hotel where so many of my Ontario friends on the other side gathered on December 9, and bear in mind that the report came out on December 29. In his bid for leadership of the provincial party, at a convention where Bren guns and federal matters were not apropos unless they were dragged in for political purposes, this young man made a startling statement. This time I quote from the Toronto Telegram. Some of my hon. friends were there, and to their credit I believe their hearts stood still and they were shocked when they heard this utterance. The leader of the opposition smiles his usual bland and delightful smile. If he was in the room and did not rise and protest he should be ashamed of himself. At this time all the evidence was in; the commissioner was doing his best to make up his mind, to deal with a difficult task and prepare his report, and this is what this young gentleman said:
You have heard of the Bren gun inquiry.
It does not say, "cheers," but the reporter may have missed the cheers.
There is no doubt what is going to happen on that subject. There will be no Bren gun contract with the government when the next session opens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: He is a prophet.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Ordering the judge.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Well, what was it? In the first place it was an 'arrant falsehood. Does anybody quarrel with that statement? In the second place it was a bid for provincial leadership. Does anybody quarrel with that statement? In the third place-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: He was then the leader.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I know the hon. member wants to be fair. I was at that convention, and this was after the convention was over.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order.

Bren Gun-Mr. Slaght

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was the night meeting, after he was appointed leader.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is one gentleman who was there. Did he rise and say, " How do you know?" Did he say, " You are discussing a matter that is sub judice?" Did he say,
" Look out, Mr. Drew; your statement is going to be published in every newspaper in Germany to-morrow morning?" No, he did not say that.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: He made the statement after he was appointed leader.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well then, it is all the worse, because it ties the hon. member in *with him. I assume the hon. member was a supporter of his, in his acquiring leadership.
Let me then in all seriousness point out to the house what happened. If he had had his way he would have shut the Inglis plant for the four months. He could not do it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, " Hear, hear." May I name him, because I want his name on Hansard. The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) says, " Hear hear," that the Inglis plant should have been closed for four months, when the British war office were urging by telegram, and everything else, " Get out those Bren guns as fast as you can."
But that was not all. The torch was thrown to the boys at Ottawa-" Let us cancel the contract."

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: " The Shadow knows."

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
" Let us cancel the contract." Eight months of production, which Mr. Gillespie says has been right up to date- one hundred per cent-although I did not read further extracts in which he said that the contract is right up to the minute. But the statement is there. The torch is thrown to Ottawa, and to my amazement and surprise hon. gentlemen opposite want now to cancel the Bren gun contract with the Inglis company.
I wonder if the five friends of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, knowing his views on patronage, which the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) exposed this afternoon, whispered to him, " Let us get this contract cancelled-out of the way. We would like to nibble at it."

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What five friends?
Mr.. SLAGHT: The five gentlemen whose names the hon. member refused to disclose; the gentlemen who were jealous, apparently,
because they could not get a chance at it, the contract. How can I name his five friends, when he is ashamed to name them himself?
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is much more I can show to you, but-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: What have you shown?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Nothing.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let me digress to say this-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member is a
virile young member of the house, and I like him and his interruptions. I want to say before I am shut off that, having regard to the situation in Canada to-day, I believe the position of the two groups in the opposite corner of the house is entirely different from that of the Conservative party opposite.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They are playing
politics.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Of course they are playing politics. I believe that the report of the commissioner was one which made it perfectly proper and right for my hon. friends in the far corner to ask parliament to look further into the matter. I regret we are going to waste time to do so. Someone has said we have most of the facts, but my friends are within their rights, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was gracious enough to say that they could have his support. I do not want anything I say to-night which shows the history of an infamous cabal to apply at all to either of the groups opposite to my right.
Now, let me say just a word about two friends of mine, the first of whom is the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton). Just a word as to him. I suggest his whole course in the matter, as disclosed by the sworn testimony, has been actuated by one motive, and one motive alone, namely the desire to serve his own people in Trinity constituency in Toronto. He has been completely vindicated by a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. Is it for that desire that he is to be pilloried and torn to pieces, with barbed and poisonous insinuations-the imaginings in which the leader of the opposition said he deals. His imagination led him to paint a vivid picture of things that the learned judge did not say. He could not quarrel with the things the learned judge did say. With all his fire and eloquence he was pointing to the wall behind me, and he had me turning round in my seat to look at the five portraits the judge had painted.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Did the hon. member see any of them?

Bren Gun-Mr. Slaght

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, I did not see any of them; that is the point. And without the slightest desire to be offensive let me suggest to the hon. member that he is suffering from "political delirium tremens." In another month we shall find him pointing to rats under his chair.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is that what one sees when one has delirium tremens?
Some .hon. MEMBERS: Time.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend is a greater authority than I am. I never have enjoyed the privilege of having that disease, and I know he never has.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then I would say my hon. friend is very lucky.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: There is a cure for it; if you are suffering from it, you can be cured.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Pink elephants.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: But to be cured you must repent, and to repent you must confess. Repentance without confession is an empty vessel. One way for my hon. friend to confess is to confess his political sins to the Speaker of the house. And I will invite him. on a future occasion when we deal with tariff matters, to make full repentance and to endeavour then, if he can, to get absolution from the people of Canada.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I wonder-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Time.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitated
to interrupt the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) while he was speaking, but I understand from the rules of order that it is unparliamentary to impute motives to any members. He stated repeatedly during his speech that those of us on this side of the house who have spoken spoke from purely political motives. I ask that that statement be withdrawn. I refer to standing order 41, citation 297, which reads:
The imputation of bad motives, or motives different from those acknowledged, misrepresenting the language of another-
And so on. The remarks of the hon. member were unparliamentary and called for prompt interference, and I ask the hon. member to withdraw.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: -of speaking from purely political motives.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member for Parry Sound did not mention the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Even that would not be out of order. Speaking from political motives is not out of order, and I wish that no other motives could be attributed to me.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion to refer this contract to the standing committee on public accounts. As I understand the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), along with the contract will go the auditor general's report. In my opinion the Bren gun contract which we are now discussing is in effect only an incident. It seems to me that this house is now under an obligation to look into other phases of the expenditures of the Department of National Defence. We can begin where the Davis report left off.
I do not propose to follow the hon. member who has just taken his seat except to say that learned counsel as he is, he played up a few arguments which might possibly catch the ears of his listeners. I would merely point out that he made a great play of the fact that interference with this contract would result in slowing up the British rearmament program. Has he read the contract? If he has he knows that it calls for the first delivery of guns in twenty-four or thirty-six months. That being the case, how can any action of this parliament at this time slow up- the delivery if, as we have been told, this concern is ready, willing and able to manufacture machine guns for delivery to the government ?
I contend that in the light of the existing records of the department, of this house and of the interdepartmental committee from which the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) quoted this afternoon, the matter of the Bren gun would seem to be most extraordinary. In view also of the replies which have been given at various times to questions asked in this house, one is forced to the conclusion that the minister either paid little attention to the affairs, of his department and signed important documents without understanding them, or failed to give this house proper and adequate information when called upon to do so. As a matter of fact,.

Bren Gun-Mr. Coldwell
I believe that the first mention of the Bren gun in this house was made by myself almost two years ago. I find that on February 22, 1937, after discussing rumours that certain factories were to be called upon to make munitions, I asked a question of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). As reported on page 1108 of Hansard of that year I said:
.	.	. are we experimenting with any guns
produced in Czechoslovakia? X have in mind the Bren machine gun. If so, what are we paying for these guns?
To this question the minister replied as follows:
I believe it was the year before last that two were ordered by the department; ten more are now on order. The Bren is a new automatic machine gun which up to now has been manufactured in Czechoslovakia. I understand that the rights of the manufacturer have been purchased by the British government and that they are to construct as soon as possible a factory in the United Kingdom for the extensive production of that type of gun. The department has been looking into the question with a view to having the gun manufactured in Canada.
The minister said that the department had been looking into the question with a view to haying the gun manufactured in Canada. As a matter of fact, the Davis report shows that the high commissioner wrote from London on February 27, 1936, a year before, concerning this particular matter. AVe find the following on page four of the report:
By letter dated February 27, 1936 (exhibit 68) the office of the High Commissioner for Canada in London advised the Secretary of State for External Affairs of the Canadian government that in connection with the adoption of the Bren light machine gun by the British army an agreement, dated May 24,
1935,	had been made by the secretary of state for the war department with the patentee embodying the terms and conditions under which the gun could be used and manufactured by the secretary of state for war and a copy of this agreement, together with a copy of a letter from the war office dated February 26,
1936,	were enclosed. Particular attention was drawn, in the high commissioner's letter, to the statement in the war office letter that in making the agreement opportunity was taken of including therein provision to enable his majesty's governments in the dominions, in the event of their adoption of the gun, to take advantage of the terms of the agreement should they desire to do so. The agreement covered the patented invention for the machine gun itself as well as a certain tripod from which the gun could be fired and a filling machine for use in connection with the gun. One of the conditions of the said agreement relating to the possible manufacture of the said gun by the dominions was that
such manufacture shall be in a factory operated by the government in question.
The statement "such manufacture shall be in a factory operated by the government in question" stands out in the report. The Davis report goes on to say on page five:
As early at least as June 3, 1936, the actual requirements for Canadian defence were put at approximately 7,000 of these guns.
The minister stated that the Bren gun production was our most vital necessity in the Dominion of Canada. Nearly nine months later he merely stated that the department had been looking into the matter, and a little later, on the same evening, February 22, 1937, I asked the minister:
AVhat company has secured the manufacturing rights of the Bren gun?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver):	None so far.
Several have been endeavouring to do so.
That is, to manufacture the Bren gun in Canada.
Let us now turn to the report of the Davis commission, and what do we find? The minister stated on the stand that no one had asked for an opportunity to manufacture the Bren gun. I ask, having in mind those two statements, how can it be said that the evidence given before the Davis commission was correct? Or, if the minister on the occasion of his appearance before the Davis commission was giving an accurate statement of what was a fact, why were we told in the House of Commons a year and a half before that there were persons who were desirous of manufacturing the gun? I say, as my leader pointed out in relation to the questions which he asked last June, that the answers are grossly inaccurate and misleading.
Now let me turn to the evidence, where we find this, that following the interview with Messrs. Cameron, Hahn and Plaxton, the minister wrote the following letter-I am quoting from page 19 of the report, but first let me read the introductory paragraph:
Following upon the interview with the minister on October 19, 1936-
That is the interview to which I have just referred.
-and without waiting for the report of the inspector who had been asked by the department on October 10 to inspect the Inglis plant in Toronto, there was sent by the deputy minister of national defence to the under secretary of state for external affairs on October 20, 1936, the following letter (exhibit 74) suggesting, in view of Major Hahn's early departure for England, the desirability of communicating with the high commissioner as soon as possible.
Then follows the letter:
Sir,-
I have the honour to refer to previous correspondence pertaining to the Bren light machine gun, following on which the Department of
Bren Gun-Mr. Coldwell

National Defence has been investigating the question of the manufacture of this gun in Canada. Major J. E. Hahn, D.S.O., M.C., a former officer of the Canadian expeditionary force, and representing a reliable group which controls certain manufacturing plants capable of manufacturing armament and munitions located in a large industrial centre where the labour and material factor is stable and favourable, has been in communication with the department.
I would draw again particular attention to the phraseology-"a reliable group which controls certain manufacturing plants"-when as a matter of fact the group was not known to the minister or known, apparently, even to the deputy minister, and moreover when it did not possess a single plant equipped to manufacture the Bren light machine gun. I say that this statement sent overseas was certainly misleading. A little later in the same letter we find this:
In this connection the department must consider the possibility of the gun being manufactured in a plant or plants other than government owned, such as for example those controlled by Major Hahn and his associates.
If ever a misleading communication were forwarded from the Dominion of Canada to the motherland, certainly this communication was of all of them one of the most misleading, and I say that on that account alone the deputy minister should be disciplined, and that the minister, who says that he takes responsibility for this letter, was either ignorant of the facts, negligent of his duty, or incompetent, and therefore should not continue to hold the position which he holds to-day.
That I submit, Mr. Speaker, is the only conclusion which can be drawn from the evidence and from this letter in particular. Why, it implies that Major Hahn and his associates had plants and were a reliable group. How did the minister or the deputy minister know that they were even financially reliable; for it was not until May, 1938, that confirmation of financial reliability of Major Hahn was submitted in a letter from the Bank of Montreal. And yet in the face of those facts we have a letter of introduction going out which, to my mind, was a strong recommendation of Major Hahn and his associates.
Moreover, what plant had they? This letter is dated October 20, 1936, and it was not until the day before, according to the report, that the representative of the bondholders accepted the offer made by the Hahn interests for the Inglis plant. Moreover the plant was being investigated by an inspector under the department. His report was already on the way, available in a day or so, and yet in the face of what must have been knowledge that this report was in hand, this letter was sent

out for the guidance of those overseas who would have something to do with the placing of the contract.
So I say that when on the other side of the house it is said that the Davis report is a vindication of the minister and of his department, it would seem to my mind to be, on the other hand, a serious questioning of the minister and of his department; and we who are members of this parliament are called upon to adjudge the issue. I want to say to hon. gentlemen opposite that speeches of the type we have heard to-night will not help because in those speeches the points at issue are not taken up. This afternoon we enjoyed the sallies of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), but he did nothing to refute the arguments of those who have condemned this contract. To-night we heard the hon. gentleman who preceded me, the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), who, as I said earlier, like a clever counsel, was quite obviously doing his best with a bad case.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
His speech will be
remembered long after that of the hon. member.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is quite possible. It will be remembered by those who delight in that kind of cheap political claptrap.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman whether he considers absolute proof that the men loaned by the British war office regarded this plant as suited to the purpose, as cheap political claptrap?
