It seems to me that the Bren gun contract has served a useful purpose in bringing before this house the necessity of careful inquiry into expenditures that have been made or are about to be made by the present Minister of National Defence. Millions of dollars have been appropriated for defence since the war; many millions have been appropriated in the last two years, and yet over and over again we are told that this country is defenceless. Is it not about time that parliament made a thorough inquiry and investigation into how these expenditures are made, and into those who are responsible for making them? I say that inquiry into this contract is necessary because perhaps it may become a typical contract, and we do not want that to happen. That is why I am warmly in support of the motion of my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil).
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) last evening criticized us for opposing increased defence estimates. At page 682 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
And when this government came to the house during the first session of this parliament to ask for $25,000,000 for national defence, what was the position taken by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) ? What was the position taken by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) ? What was the position taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) ? The minister will perhaps remember when I remind him what that attitude was, and I will quote from Hansard of 1937. When the hon. member for Vancouver North spoke he made a statement on behalf of the group with which he is associated and at page 882 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
I submit that one of the first and most necessary contributions to national defence, and one that should be made before we pay over additional millions, is so to purge the present establishment as to place it on a businesslike and sensible basis. Eliminate patronage, social nonsense and obsolete military routine and there might be some opportunity for men in that department to do something, men who have some technical knowledge and grasp of the requirements of national defence. If the country wants defence, there might then be some hope of its getting money for its money.
That was one of the grounds upon which we opposed those estimates; and if hon. members will look through the discussions during these three years they will find that
points similar to those contained in the statement which I have just read were made over and over again by members of this group. The second point upon which we opposed the estimates was the fact that no one knew exactly how these armaments were going to be used, what the foreign policy of the government was, or what the policy of the British administration which the government was following happened to be.
Last night the Minister of Agriculture quoted Sir Thomas Inskip as he spoke on July 20, 1936, in the British House of Commons. The minister said that he was there. I ask him, did he hear the speech which immediately preceded that of Sir Thomas Inskip, the speech of the leader of the Liberal party in Great Britain, Sir Archibald Sinclair? It is strange to me that in debates on foreign policy the government of Canada, which calls itself Liberal, always quotes the leaders of illiberalism in Great Britain. I have before me what Sir Archibald Sinclair said and I am going to put it on the record. Sir Archibald, in the summer of 1936, said almost in identical language exactly what this group has said in this house in connection with our defence estimates.

The minister stated last night that we in this group had consistently opposed the defence estimates, and asked upon what grounds we opposed them. I point to the two main grounds that I have given, and they will be found embodied in the records of this house. In my opinion no group criticizing any estimates has ever had a clearer vindication of their opposition than can be found in the report of the Davis commission. It is all very well to say that the report found no one guilty of misconduct. That is not what the commission was charged with doing. The form was reported upon; "the form, not the substance, of the contract." Upon the substance we in this house, and through us the people of this dominion, must judge. So our attitude on defence estimates throughout has been vindicated by what we are now discussing.
In closing I say that a matter of this kind at the present time in the Dominion of Canada, or in any other democratic country, is to be deplored, because it tends to undermine faith in our democratic institutions and in those who are charged with the responsibilities of government. Matters of this sort do more to undermine what we loosely term democracy than all the propaganda that can be sent from over the seas. It enables some to point the finger of scorn at parliament, and to say, what we need is a certain type of so-called big business men in this house. I venture to say that those who would institute the rule of big business would also stifle free discussion.
I am persuaded that if we want to continue the institution of parliament, we who are [Mr. M. McLean.)
within these walls at the present time must judge a matter of this kind not from any preconceived notions that we may have but according to the material before us. In my opinion the commissioner places the questions clearly before this house, and we have to answer them. Be that as it may, I say that at least the report of the commissioner, the evidence given before him and the airing which has been given to the evidence in this house this week, have certainly undermined the confidence of the people of Canada in the Minister of National Defence and in those who serve immediately under him. I think it probable that until this debate occurred in this house the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was not altogether aware of all that was in the evidence and in this report. I am quite sure that many hon. members were not conversant with it. Those of us who had read some of the evidence-I had not read all of it for there are many volumes-have from hour to hour during the past two days heard evidence and conclusions based upon that evidence of which we had no knowledge before. So I am urging that the motion now before the house be adopted, and that, not a rehash of the evidence given before the Davis commission be undertaken, but that the operations of the Department of National Defence under the present minister and those who serve immediately under him be thoroughly inquired into by the public accounts committee.

I do not rise for the purpose of defending Colonel Drew; he has shown on many occasions that he is quite capable of looking after himself. The fact of the

The hon. member for Parry Sound made reference to Mr. Gillespie's evidence. So did the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). What did Mr.' Gillespie say? He said that these men had the ability to produce Bren guns. So have fifty other men in Canada, one hundred per cent ability to produce them. Mr. Gillespie did not say they were in a position to do so; he did say they had the ability to do so. The hon. member for Parry Sound challenged us to say whether or not we would say that the factory should be closed. I said yes, and I say it again. The people of Canada will say, "Close the factory." There are many Liberal members in this house who wish this thing had never occurred. When the hon. member for Parry Sound speaks so much of the British empire and our responsibility in helping to produce guns to defend that empire, let me say this: God help the empire if they are going to depend for their defence on some Bren guns delivered in twenty-four or twenty-six months from now.
It is^ difficult for any hon. member, from his place in this house, to discuss certain phases of government business which, unfortunately, have caused the people of this country to think there is something materially wrong m_ the Department of National Defence and with those men to whom we entrust such important questions. For many years, ever since confederation in fact, we have had prime ministers with characters above reproach, and in that category I include the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He knows only too well, however, that there are times when those who support piime ministers are not always as careful as they should be in their governmental actions. In this particular instance I do not believe the Prime Minister was cognizant of what was going on. He was not told the truth; he was kept in the dark. But I do say this about him, that after he had declared the policy of the Liberal party in connection with a matter which was of such prime importance to Canada and the empire, this was one matter to which he should have given exceptional scrutiny before he ever became a party to the signing of a contract such as this.
What precipitated this whole mess, because that is what it is to my mind? It was the
Drew article in .Maclean's magazine. It was admitted in evidence that as a result of the publication of this article, one clause was cleared up within a day or two, which action it is quite generally understood saved this country and this government the sum of $250,000.

So there is the story that went out across this country.
When we start to delve into the report, we begin to see just what a terrible mistake the Department of National Defence made. There are in Canada a great many industries capable of making Bren guns. They do work in steel that is much more intricate than the manufacture of a Bren gun. After all, what is there to the Bren gun? The important part is the alloy and the fact that the barrel is interchangeable. Steel companies throughout this dominion do more intricate work, and I venture to say that if they had been given an opportunity to tender on these guns the government would have obtained them for at least half the amount they are going to cost this country under this contract. More than that, these people would not have asked to be paid a large sum of money for getting government patronage, which is really what happened with Major Hahn and his associates.

It might be interjected at this point that later, on the witness stand, Major Hahn testified that an old appraisal made in October, 1929, of the old Inglis plant as a going concern, fixed the then value at $1,327,000, exclusive of land.
A first payment of $500 was made on September 22, 1936. The next payment of $2,500 was made on November 9 of the same year. A third payment of $1,000 was made on May 10, 1937. Thereafter payments ranging up to $3,500 were made at intervals, but up to the time the Bren machine gun contract was signed only $46,500 had been paid. In the meantime the new John Inglis Company had been organized. On March 31, 1938, the day the government signed the Bren gun contract, the company itself made the final payment of 353,500.
These people then made the final payment on this factory which had been represented to the British war office and to a committee here made up of civil servants as an industry equipped to make Bren guns. Of the first $46,500 of cash payments the books of Cameron, Pointon and Merritt-this is all from the evidence-credited Major James E. Hahn with $26,416.86; Gordon Plaxton with $3,616.67; Herbert Plaxton with $3,616.67, and the firm itself with $10,850. An investigation carried on by Mr. Hoult showed that these moneys were likewise applied on the books of the new Inglis company as payment on account of the undertaking of Hahn and his group to purchase 58,333 shares at $6 par value. The final payment of $53,500 on the cash purchase price of the old company's assets was made directly from the treasury of the new John Inglis Company.
Here is another point which is perfectly clear. The total capital of the new Inglis company was 250,000 shares at S6 par value, or $1,500,000. Of this $1,500,000 of capital stock Major Hahn and his group took for themselves 191,662 shares of $6 par value, or a total of $1,149,972. This was stock for which they paid nothing. This stock has been termed vendors' stock. Excluding five qualifying shares which were given to the nominal original directors who came from the office staff, the group left in the treasury 58,333 shares of $6 par value which they agreed to buy at par, paying in instalments. To put it more plainly, this group held seventy per cent of the total capital stock of the company-

For nothing.

speechtext:
For nothing, and they had agreed to buy the other thirty per cent and to pay the money into the treasury in order to operate the company. This money was to go into the treasury to operate the company; yet the government was buying all the machinery for the plant. These people had all these shares for nothing, and then they were going to buy the others in order to-put money into the company with which to operate. Who would not take a contract like that from a government? I wish I could get two or three to-morrow.
May we go on? Up to September 15, 1938, it was shown that the group had paid in $231,198 on the 58,333 shares of $6 treasury stock which had a total value of $349,998, which they were obligated to buy. On that date they owned outright a $1,500,000 corporation, its assets and stock for that amount of money, subject to the payment of a balance of $118,000 on the treasury stock. The initial cash payment of $100,000 had been charged against these treasury funds. In the meantime 3,855 shares of treasury stock had been sold to the public and a few brokers for $27,041. The public paid $7.50 a share for its stock. It is easy to fill in the details when you get the framework.
Though the Hahn-Inglis corporation set-up was engineered with four corporations, one functioned only to take the group s subscription for $349,998 of treasury stock. Another functioned as a temporary holding company for the huge block of $1,149,972 of vendor's shares taken by the group. The third corporation was the machine which 'created the stock expansion, and the fourth was converted into the John Inglis Company. There is the picture. If ever there was a piece of manipulation for the purpose of watering stock of a company, this gives the picture. This is something to which western members can point with pride. They can point to this as showing how their government gives a large contract. I have given the exact picture of this whole affair.
The stock expansion corporation was the British Canadian Engineering Company which was incorporated on November 23, 1936, with an authorized capital of 200,000 shares at $1 each. Mr. Nurse, an employee of Cameron, Pointon and Merritt, who had bought in the old Inglis property, made an agreement, of date October 22, 1936, with Major J. E. Hahn and his employers to turn over to this British Canadian Engineering Company, when incorporated, the properties of the old Inglis company. One interesting paragraph in this

Bren Gun-Mr. Bertrand (Laurier)
early agreement of October 22, 1936, made nearly eighteen months before the Bren gun contract was signed, reads:
John E>. Cameron, H. A. W. (Herbert) Plaxton and the persons they represent, together with Major Hahn "are interested to manufacture war machinery, equipment, munitions and supplies or products of all kinds, and to act as agents, intermediaries or otherwise in obtaining, introducing or placing business or orders for war machinery, equipment, munitions and supplies or products of all kinds as may be furnished, dealt in, manufactured or supplied by other persons, firms or corporations whether in the United Kingdom, dominion of Canada, United States of America or elsewhere, and the parties hereto have agreed to incorporate, organize and promote a limited company for the above purpose."
In other words, these people were organized to make munitions, and in this contract there is nothing which says that they cannot use the Canadian government's machinery to make munitions for some foreign power. When one follows this thing through one begins to realize that here was a group of men without a plant and without any particular engineering ability. One had been mixed up with a radio company and the others were lawyers and brokers. These men come to this government, and the government points to ,them and says to the British war office, "Here are the only men who are capable of making Bren guns in Canada." If ever there was an insult to the heads of industry in this country, that was it. All one has to do is read the contract. Read what the deputy minister of defence said in his evidence. Read what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) said in his evidence. Read what some hon. members opposite have said in the house. One cannot help but feel that these men considered the heads of industry and the workmen in industry in this dominion absolutely incompetent to do a job like that.
As the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) said this afternoon, manufacturers come to Ottawa to see all departments of government. They pay their own expenses to come here to bid on contracts in order to get government business. All this government had to do was to say to the steel manufacturers of this country: We want these guns made and we want other arms and munitions made. These men would have come here. The heads of industries in Canada are loyal enough to give of their time, of their experts and of their office staffs and to spend their money to help the Department of National Defence to build up an effective defence force. Yet the Minister of National Defence and the deputy minister of national defence say to our Canadian manufacturers: You are not
competent; we cannot trust you with this job; it is too intricate a job for you, and we are going to give it to a man who had a radio company that failed, to a couple of brokers and a couple of lawyers, and the patronage is going to a member from the city of Toronto. That is the story in a nutshell.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the members of this house cannot help but feel that the contract is not only improvident but unfair to the Department of National Defence, because it is going to be years before we get guns. They are now buying the machinery in spite of the Davis report. The government would not wait. Mr. Justice Davis in his report did not exonerate the government from responsibility for the contract. Corruption, no; he said there was no corruption. That is quite true, but he did not exonerate the government in any other way. What he did say to them was this: Here is your baby; this is your child. In a very subtle way he said: It is a little dirty and messy; it ought to be cleaned up, and it is up to parliament and the government to do the job.
There is only one way to do the job, Mr. Speaker, and that is to cancel the contract. I think the Prime Minister himself should unhesitatingly say: I will agree to cancel the contract and to create a munitions board. Not a purchasing board, Mr. Speaker, because patronage would be just as vicious under a purchasing board. But let the Prime Minister and his government say: We will create a munitions board and give them the right to handle the whole business, so that we can clean this thing up and once more give the people of Canada some confidence in the Department of National Defence.

There are very few high officials of this government who enjoy a higher reputation than my friend Major General LaFleche. From the fall of 1914, when he attended his military school to get his lieutenancy, right down until to-day with the high rank he has now attained, his life has been, I think, a true expression of patriotism and of outright devotion to his king and country, and to his position he brings a very well-balanced intelligence and devouring energy. It would take more than the libellous pen of Colonel Drew to break that reputation so far as we are concerned, and we all applaud Judge Davis when he says in his report:
I think it right to say that there is no evidence (nor is there in the evidence any ground for suspicion) that the minister or the deputy minister or any officer or official of the Department of National Defence was guilty of any act of corruption or anything in the nature of corruption.
And it is well for the hon. minister to say that corruption has never been charged against anybody. They are going into their second trench of defence. When this article of Colonel Drew's came out, rumours were going around that there was a mighty scandal in this affair, and that Colonel Drew would prove it. We have the idea that this attempt to discredit Major General LaFleche is due to the fact that Colonel Drew and the Tories, and especially the Tories of his species, because there are good Tories, could not reconcile their ideas with the fact that Major General LaFleche is the head of a big spending department and yet of French extraction.

All right,

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is filthy stuff.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The rumour
was all around that there was going to be an attack upon General LaFleche. The hon. leader of the opposition was not in the house then.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I never knew of any such thing.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I said the
hon. gentleman was not in the house. Well,

it came out this year; it came out, if you will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, like an abscess, and it is not surprising because Colonel Drew is the man who said in Plainfield, Ontario, in November, 1936:
It is not unfair to remind the French that they are a defeated race and that their rights are rights only because of the tolerance by the English element who, with all respect to the minority, must be regarded as the dominant race.
We put two and two together; we put this together with the rumour that we heard last year.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think in justice to an
absent gentleman, and a man who is just as courageous as General LaFleche, it should be said that Colonel Drew has denied that over and over again, and his denial has been accepted. There is an attempt being made now to make this an attack on the French Canadians. My wife is a French Canadian, and I would be ashamed to have anything to do with an attack on her race. I think it is filthy to attempt any such thing as my hon. friend is doing right now.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Colonel
Drew is not here to deny it. This statement that I have read has been published in every newspaper and I never saw a denial of it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
He has denied it many
times.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well, I
think he should deny it once more. All through his article that we were called upon to read before it appeared in the magazine there appeared to be jealousy of the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) and of his deputy minister, who have started doing something for national defence.
Several years ago Colonel Drew wrote that nothing was being done with regard to the defence of Canada, and as soon as something is started he condemns it. I have read the charge before the commission, and I have never found so many silly arguments put. together, all of which prove the futility of his accusations. One of his points is that the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) tried to deceive the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) because, when he talked about this affair, he wrote " plants," plural, instead of " plant," singular, in his letter, although there are eighty acres of buildings in the old Inglis plant.
There are quite a number of arguments like that in Colonel Drew's charge before the commission, but I shall not take up the time of the house in discussing them. It has been said that a promoter is a man who, having

Bren Gun-Mr. Bertrand (Laurier)
an idea, meets another man who has money and seeks to deal with him, with the result that the man who has the money is left with the idea and the man who has the idea is left with the money. Colonel Drew, I understand, was superintendent under the Security Frauds Prevention Act, and this definition, in the work he had to do, must have stuck somewhere in his brain, because the main crime of Major Hahn and his group seemed to be that they were promoters. I am quite sure that Colonel Drew illustrates the meaning of the word " promoter " which I have just given to the house.
I wish to put on Hansard what the late Sir James MacBrien said about Major Hahn. Of course, to-day some hon. members who are attacking the contract are not aware of what Sir James MacBrien thought of Major Hahn. Let me quote Sir James MacBrien:
It will be a source of satisfaction to many Canadians who served at the front in the recent war to learn that a book on The Intelligence Service within the Canadian corps has been written by Major J. E. Hahn, D.S.O., M.C. There are few Canadian soldiers so well qualified as he to write a book on this important branch of the military work as it was organized, developed and carried out in the Canadian corps during the course of the great war. His record at the front was a brilliant one. Except for periods when he was incapacitated through wounds, he served continuously with.the Canadians in France and Belgium, and he has the honour of being one of the original members of the first Canadian division. A considerable portion of his service was as an intelligence staff officer with various formations, where he learned in the school of practical experience. Therefore, he brings special and valuable knowledge to bear on the subject of which he writes.
I wanted to put this on the record because of the attack that has been made against Major Hahn. The fact that a man was at one time a radio manufacturer, in the bad days while hon. gentlemen on the other side were leading the affairs of the country, with the result that his business went into receivership, is no reason why he should be blamed. I quite understand that these hon. gentlemen, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members, who are trying to have the greatest human quality, ambition, disappear from this good earth, are continually branding successful business men as public enemy No. 1, 2 or 3. I can understand that they might yell " shame." They are so narrow-minded that they would not even allow a business man to earn the income tax which they will require him to pay if, as and when they get into power.
Major Hahn got my friend the hon. member for Trinity to introduce him to the Minister of National Defence in order to *et the contract. Where is the hon. member
who has not solicited government contracts for some of his constituents? Is not a contract like the Bren gun one the best thing that could be secured for a constituency in which there is a labour element, such as Trinity? Let the electors of Trinity answer the question in the near future; but I do not advise Colonel Drew to run in Trinity in the next general election for the federal house, nor do I advise him to approach the district in the provincial field.
The question is not whether the contract should have been given to somebody else; it is whether there is ground for suspicion in the granting of the contract. I quoted the words of Mr. Justice Davis as to suspicion. The only points at issue, all of which have been answered by the commissioner to the complete exoneration of the Minister of National Defence and of everyone concerned, are the following: Is the contract a good one for the government? Is it being carried out according to schedule? And was the government right in not calling for public tenders?
The government had machinery that was idle in Valcartier and the government needed Bren machine guns. It would have cost a tremendous amount of money to build a government-owned plant, which might have been put only to temporary use. Every business man will understand that such a plant owned by the government could not have been used for anything but arms and munitions, and that the plant could not have been used to compete in the production of any ordinary line of steel products as against private producers. In this case the overhead expenses would have been exceedingly high, almost prohibitive. It was necessary to induce a manufacturer whose overhead expenses were partly absorbed by the manufacturing of some other goods to enter into a contract, and Major Hahn was found to be the proper man.
The statement to the public that the John Inglis Company had reorganized solely for the Bren gun contract is a premeditated misrepresentation. The commercial budget for the next five years provides for a business which is almost as high, apart from the Bren gun contract, as was done in the last good years of the John Inglis Company. It was furthermore discovered that the Canadian government and the company would both greatly benefit should a contract be obtained from the imperial government, then in dire need of help for the manufacture of arms and munitions. Major Hahn went to England with the necessary credentials to deal with the war office. He was found trustworthy and able to fulfil a contract for the manufacture of 5,000 machine guns. It is absolutely impossible to
736	COMMONS
Bren Gun-Mr. Bertrand (Laurier)
criticize this Canadian contract without at the same time criticizing the imperial contract. It has no bearing on the case, that Major Hahn went to England with the hon. member for Trinity or anyone else, or whether he waited five, ten or fifteen days before presenting his credentials. The net result is that he succeeded in bringing to Canada a good contract, which, coupled with the Canadian contract, will provide in Toronto a new industry and work for the citizens and at the same time lend a helping hand to the harassed war office.
During the inquiry an attempt was made to leave the public under the impression that the Department of National Defence had made a gift of the Valcartier machinery to the company; the hon. member who spoke before me (Mr. Homuth) repeated somewhat the same thing. Nothing is more-I would say more cowardly false. The machinery is lent to the company and, with the new machinery, remains entirely the property of the Canadian government. No hon. member has mentioned that in this discussion. Although one-third of the cost of the new machinery is paid by the war office, it remains the property of the Canadian government when the contract is terminated; and one-third of the cost of tools, et cetera is also paid by the war office, although they remain the property of the Canadian government. The Ross rifle plant furnished about one hundred machines out of four hundred required for the fulfilment of the contract. The Ross rifle machinery is valued at $212,000, while the new machinery is worth $964,000. By the signing of the contract the Canadian government immediately gained one-third of this amount, that is $321,000, plus one-third of the tools, dies, et cetera, worth more than $200,000. The argument that the government pays for everything, and a profit in addition, is childish in the light of these facts, and would not deceive even a village half-wit. What does it matter whether the government pays half the cost of the machinery or all of it? The profit is calculated on the cost, but the rental value of the machinery belonging to the government does not enter into consideration so far as the cost of production is concerned. This is one thing that hon. members who criticize the contract do not dare to say. The cost is calculated on the company's share of the assets only, not on the government's portion. If the plant and machinery were the property of the government, the profit would be calculated only on the cost of raw material, wages, and part of the overhead. It is absolutely unfair to compare this, a cost-
plus contract, with a contract that a manufacturer would obtain if he were coming here. On a cost-plus contract the government has to pay all the cost, even the expenses of the man who went over th.ere to learn what the Bren gun was. Now Mr. Sharp of the income tax branch calculated that the maximum profit would be 7-76 per cent, which is less than a reasonable profit in that kind of industry, as every business man will agree. Beyond all this there is a stipulation as to the maximum possible profit, $267,000, which is substantially less than 10 per cent.
Suffice it to say that Judge Davis, who cannot be said to be in the remotest way partial to this government, made three findings that have not been referred to by hon. members on the other side. These are that the contract was not subject to suspicion; that there were adequate powers of inspection, supervision and control; and that no substantial objection could be taken to the provisions of the contract. In view of this it cannot be said that the contract is not a good one for the government, as in fact it was found to be by the commissioner. In a cost-plus contract any good business man would charge depreciation on his machinery, and a fair rental value. Instead of being a gift to the John Inglis Company the use of the government's machinery reduces the cost and therefore reduces the profit. That made the Department of National Defence a partner in the contract. This is one point that I would ask my hon. friends the social crediters to remember, because that the government should own the plant is their ideal. Under this contract we can well say that Major Hahn is simply an employee of the government, working on a job basis. Everything belongs to the government except the machinery that was there which is going to be used.
It is a good contract. In spite of the fact that the inquiry was a serious handicap to its fulfilment, and that Colonel Drew and so many others asked that the work be stopped, work has been proceeding at high speed. Major Hahn got hold of Mr. Gillespie, the best expert of the Enfield plant, who had already planned the production of Bren guns in England, and the work under the contract is right up to schedule. When hon. gentlemen criticize and say they are simply putting the machine on in the plant, they are not absolutely fair. This is one contract, but it may well be divided into two. The simple fact of collecting all this machinery, assembling it and putting it to work is a big undertaking in itself. If it had to be done afresh it would

Bren Gun-Mr. Bertrand (Laurier)
take at least a year and a half or two years to get this plant together and ready to operate. There was no similar plant in Canada. When one considers the importance to Great Britain of having these Bren guns in the shortest time humanly possible, are we not justified in saying that the meagre pay given to Colonel Drew for his magazine article seems like treason money? It is not surprising that Colonel Drew's name is so well known in fascist circles in Canada. I suppose this is another statement that Colonel Drew will deny; but pamphlets were circulated in my province, and I have one here, in which Colonel Drew is named as one of the adepts of the fascist movement in Canada. This booklet is entitled, "Fascism over Canada," an expose by Fred Rose, and on page 45 I read this:
But Arcand and the forces of reaction have many other supporters in high places. Colonel George A. Drew is one of the people who is working for an alliance with Hepburn in Ontario and for a national government in Canada that would pave the way for fascism. The colonel travels from place to place, and under the guise of defending democracy, slanders most viciously all true democrats. Mr. Drew is honorary president of the Canadian Unity League, an organization financed by International Nickel for the purpose of combating trade union organizations. Such anti-labour organizations, using different names, exist throughout the country and are closely linked with the fascist movement.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I ask the
hop. gentleman if that is by Fred Rose, the communist writer?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear. No doubt it is.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not
know Fred Rose, the communist writer. .1 know Fred Rose who wrote this book; I do not think he is a communist. If he is, I am sui-prised at the hon. member asking me; he should tell me whether he is a communist or not.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member
will be padlocked.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not afraid.
Was the government justified in not calling for tenders? To have an idea of what delay-means in this matter I might say that twenty-one Bren guns were ordered by the national defence department from England at the beginning of March, 1937, and they were delivered in January of this year, although pressure was applied to expedite the order. One must keep in mind that this government had to deal with the war office and could not open the secret specifications and manufacturing processes to any firms that were not first accepted by the war office.
On February 4, 1938, Sir Harold Brown calbled Colonel LaFleche as follows:
Must emphasize that any further delay may adversely affect the proposal. In this connection firm having done necessary technical investigation obviously has the advantage.
That firm was Major Hahn's. Then Colonel Loggie cabled General Caldwell as follows:
Re visit war office affecting gun I am of firm opinion that immediate action is essential and that any delay will jeopardize whole transaction.
These gentlemen who were representing the war office were in a hurry, much more so than was Colonel Drew, who wanted to close the plant here. The war office made it absolutely clear, in February, 1938, in a cable sent by Sir Harold Brown to the deputy minister of national defence:
as regards alternative tenders several months would necessarily be required for another firm to study job before making reasonable tender. This delay would be fatal to British interests in scheme.
These three cables have not been mentioned very often by those who criticize the contract; yet they are the three things that explain why bids could not be invited from the general public. There had been an extended correspondence for the purpose of obtaining the consent of the British government to the calling of tenders. Before Hahn could get the specifications it was necessary to make him an official representative of the Canadian government; otherwise the war office would not give them. The manufacturing processes, called working specifications in England, were only furnished to Major Hahn upon execution of the contract. They were never even nominally in the possession of the defence department until that time. I do not remember who it was that made it almost a crime for this government to nominate Major Hahn as Canadian representative in London in order to deal with the British war office. Major Hahn, with his remarkable war record, was the man designated, and he fully deserves the confidence that the Canadian government has reposed in him. As I said before, he was also found trustworthy by the imperial government which, as I understand it, was not born yesterday. When they trust somebody, and award a contract of such value, they take some care and make some investigations somewhere. It is not for us to know where they made those investigations, but we are certainly justified in giving our confidence to Major Hahn. Then Sir Harold Brown cabled General LaFleche on February 9, 1938:
Draft of Bren gun contract with John Inglis Company now- agreed in detail by war office.

They were waiting for the Canadian government to conclude its contract, and the Canadian government was assured that the imperial contract with the war office would be signed if the Canadian contract was signed. This is clear evidence that the imperial government would not allow competitive bids, and if it would not do so the national defence department could not allow them either.
I am one of those who believe we still have a good deal to learn from British methods of doing things, and I would not dare to criticize those methods in a field in which we are still in our infancy. The Tories, to whom nothing is good unless it comes straight from the British isles, are apt to forget this at times. After all, we remember the purchasing of horses and potatoes without tenders. Not only were there no tenders called; the merchants were told to sell their merchandise through middlemen. There are no secret specifications in the breeding of horses or the growing of potatoes. Therefore I say that the question of the secrecy of the specifications, the necessity of moving quickly and avoiding delays and the sine qua non condition of the imperial government left the national defence department no other alternative, and on this point, as on so many others, the commissioner has completely upheld the government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not contend that there were no other manufacturers who could have satisfied the government as to their capacity to fulfil such a contract; but there is no proof whatever that anyone else did inquire about the matter or attempt to get the contract, and I for one am absolutely satisfied with the manner in which our government exercised its discretion. If to avoid a possible charge of political patronage this present government has to sign its contracts with social crediters, C.C.F.-ers and/or Conservatives, it is going to be too bad for more than half our Canadian citizens. When it was announced over a year ago that Great Britain would have aeroplanes and munitions manufactured in Canada, I read very little criticism and a great deal of praise. If this government had not taken the appropriate steps; instead of having them manufactured in Canada we would have had to buy the Bren machine guns somewhere else, and I do not know where, because England had its hands full with it own munitions program. Canada would have lost the English contract, which, after all, is going to be a factor in the labour world. In the opinion of many business men Colonel Drew's unfounded criticism and its repercussions might have resulted in many other contracts for arms

and munitions being lost to Canadian manufacturers. So I say it is impossible to criticize this Canadian contract without explicitly criticizing the imperial contract as well.
I take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of National Defence upon his courageous stand in these difficult circumstances. National defence has been terribly neglected since the great war. No one ever thought there would rise up aggressive nations which would challenge the combined forces of democracy; but when nations such as Germany, Italy and Japan are asking for territory and threatening to invade French colonies and even part of France itself; when they call for a new distribution of wealth, meaning territories, it is time for us who have such a large territory with such a small population to realize more than ever that eternal vigilance is the price of liberty.

Bren Gun-Mr. Poole

speechtext: I would draw your attention, sir, to the fact that the hon. member who preceded me quoted from a communist newspaper.

speechtext: Had I been in the chair I would have stopped him.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We shall forget about newspaper comments for the moment, but there will be more of them in the future. The important matter before parliament at the present time is to remember the conditions which were brought about in the armament industry during the war and to see that they are not repeated. I think the best way to go about that and to see that the public shall not be victimized is for the government to cancel this contract and assume whatever loss may be incurred. I believe that would be cheaper in the long run. We should give serious consideration to utilizing the plant and equipment there is at present in Canada. Much of this is wholly or partly idle. There are manjf men in this country who have a certain training which would be useful to the production of Bren or other guns. We have the Canadian National railway shops and thousands of idle men. Surely these buildings and this labour could be utilized. We could provide our own equipment. If. that were done, there would be no necessity for investigations of this kind.
It is well known that the armament industry in general has contributed nothing toward peace, but has fomented war and internal strife wherever possible. The time to stamp out that sort of thing is now, not ten years hence. You cannot help people by expressing platitudes and regrets. Let each and every party in this house remember what occurred in the pagt and provide for the protection of the public in the future. The time to do it is now. It is an iniquitous practice, in my opinion, to let contracts privately for the manufacture of armaments. We are laying the foundations for the growth of the most insidious organization the world has ever known.
For further information in this regard I would refer the hon. members to the report of a committee which sat in the United States to study the munitions industry and report on the activities and sales of munitions companies. This report contains quite recent evidence and tells of the activities of these people at Geneva. It describes how they supplied both China and Japan with arms and furnished both sides in Spain with armaments. They are said to have fomented strife in the South American republics. There is no reason to believe that an armament industry which might be created in this country will be any different from any other armament industry.

As a matter of fact, the industry has within itself the seed of all these things. It can afford to pay thousands of dollars to lobbyists in order to persuade influential members of parliament and those in responsible positions in government to pass certain laws to give it liberty to extract its dreadful toll over a long period of years.
I said when I rose in my place that I was not going into the details of this contract. My only reason for rising was to sound a warning. While I did attempt to quote some newspaper articles, I must say that I am not impressed with all of them. I know that political advantage is taken of a matter of this kind. It is in the interests of the Liberal party to remedy the condition that exists. I feel that there are many members who sit on the government benches who believe that we should be most careful in handling the production of armaments and munitions. The time has arrived when these matters should be under the control of the government. It is in the public interest that this work should be done in our own factories. Only in that way can we be assured that there will be no recurrence of the iniquitous practices of the past.
On motion of Mr. Turgeon the debate was adjourned.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939

NATIONAL DEFENCE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEFENCE PURCHASING BOARD TO ENTER INTO CONTRACTS FOR MUNITIONS, EQUIPMENT, MATERIALS AND SUPPLIES

Defence Purchasing Board

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a defence purchasing board with exclusive power, subject to approval of the governor in council, to enter into all contracts for the purchase of munitions, equipment, materials and supplies required by the Department of National Defence in cases where the expenditure exceeds $5,000; to provide safeguards to assure that such munitions, equipment, materials and supplies shall be purchased at a reasonable cost to the government and without unreasonable profit to any manufacturer or supplier thereof; to provide that salaries, wages and other expenses of the board shall be payable out of moneys appropriated by parliament.
To authorize the governor in council to borrow such sums of money as may be required to pa}' expenditures of the Department of National Defence which are chargeable to capital account in the appropriations provided by parliament for the said department; and to provide a sinking fund sufficient to retire in ten years the said sums borrowed for capital expenditures of the said department, together with interest thereon at three per cent per annum.

General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :

Mr. Speaker, the attitude that has
been taken both by this group and by the party to my left has been taken because private members' resolutions-nobody is to blame for this-have been practically pushed off the order paper.
